name: Marduk
original: Akkadian Marduk (Sumerian AMAR.UTU, 'bull-calf of the sun'); Hebrew Bel (title 'lord') and Merodach
symbol: The mushhushshu (a scaly snake-dragon with lion forelegs and eagle hind legs) and the triangular-headed spade (marru)

cultCenter.name: Esagila temple and the Etemenanki ziggurat, Babylon

family.name: Ea (Enki), god of fresh water and wisdom

plain: Marduk was the patron god of the city of Babylon and, from about 1100 BC onward, the head of the Babylonian gods. People usually called him simply Bel, meaning 'lord' (the same word as the Canaanite title Baal). When the prophets mock 'Bel' they are mocking the chief god of the empire that destroyed Jerusalem.
myth:
Marduk's great myth is the *Enuma Elish* ('When on high'), a Babylonian creation epic probably composed in the late second millennium BC and recited at the New Year (akitu) festival. In it the older gods are threatened by Tiamat, the salt-water sea pictured as a monstrous mother. The young Marduk agrees to fight her on condition that he is made king of the gods. He catches her in a net, drives a wind into her mouth, shoots an arrow through her, and splits her body in two like a dried fish, making the sky from one half and the earth from the other. He then creates humans from the blood of Tiamat's defeated general Qingu so that people can do the gods' work, and the gods build Babylon and the Esagila temple for him. The poem ends by listing his fifty names.

The story was political as well as religious: it explained why Babylon and its god stood at the top of the world. When Babylon rose, Marduk rose with it; earlier versions of the same kind of story gave the hero's role to other gods such as Enlil or Ninurta.
biblicalRole:
Marduk appears in the Bible mainly under his title Bel, and once as Merodach. Isaiah pictures the fall of Babylon as a humiliating removal van: 'Bel bows down, Nebo stoops' — the great statues that were carried in triumphant procession at the New Year festival now have to be loaded onto tired animals and carried into captivity themselves (Isa 46:1-2). The contrast is pointed: Babylon's gods must be carried, but Israel's God carries his people (Isa 46:3-4). Jeremiah's oracle against Babylon announces that 'Bel is put to shame, Merodach is dismayed' (Jer 50:2) and that God will punish Bel in Babylon and make him spit out what he swallowed (Jer 51:44).

His name also survives inside personal names: Merodach-baladan, the Babylonian king who sent envoys to Hezekiah (Isa 39:1), and Evil-merodach (Amel-Marduk, 'man of Marduk'), who released King Jehoiachin from prison (2 Kgs 25:27). Daniel's Babylonian name Belteshazzar is said in the text to be 'according to the name of my god' (Dan 4:8); the Akkadian behind it is usually reconstructed as Balatsu-usur ('protect his life'), so the link to Bel may be a wordplay rather than a precise etymology.

Most striking of all, the Babylonian propaganda of Cyrus claimed that Marduk chose Cyrus to restore order, while Isaiah says it was Yahweh who called Cyrus 'his anointed' (Isa 45:1; Isa 44:28). Two theologies describe the same event, each crediting its own god.

encounters.title: Bel and Nebo carried off on beasts of burden
encounters.summary: Isaiah turns the New Year procession upside down: the idols that were paraded through Babylon become baggage loaded onto weary animals. The point is that a god who has to be carried cannot carry anyone.

encounters.title: Bel put to shame, Merodach shattered
encounters.summary: Jeremiah's long oracle against Babylon names its chief god directly and announces his humiliation alongside the fall of the city.

encounters.title: Cyrus: chosen by Marduk or by Yahweh?
encounters.summary: When Cyrus of Persia took Babylon in 539 BC, his own cylinder inscription said Marduk had searched for a righteous king and chosen him. The biblical writers say Yahweh stirred Cyrus's spirit. Isaiah even adds 'though you do not know me' (Isa 45:4), conceding that Cyrus was not a worshipper of Israel's God.

encounters.title: Marduk inside royal names
encounters.summary: Merodach-baladan (Marduk-apla-iddina II) courted Hezekiah as an ally against Assyria; Evil-merodach freed Jehoiachin. Both names carry the god's name, a reminder of how much Babylonian public life was bound up with him.

archaeology.place: Babylon, foundations of the Esagila area (now in the British Museum)
archaeology.summary: A clay barrel inscribed in Akkadian after Cyrus's capture of Babylon in 539 BC. It says Marduk grew angry with the last Babylonian king, Nabonidus, chose Cyrus, and let him enter Babylon without a battle; it also describes returning gods and peoples to their home sanctuaries. It does not mention the Jews, but historians widely see it as the same policy reflected in Ezra 1.

archaeology.place: Babylon (excavated by Robert Koldewey; reconstructed in Berlin)
archaeology.summary: Glazed-brick walls show rows of mushhushshu dragons, Marduk's animal, along with bulls and lions. This was the road down which Marduk's statue travelled at the New Year festival — the very procession Isa 46 mocks.

archaeology.find: Etemenanki ziggurat and the 'Tower of Babel' stele
archaeology.summary: The seven-stage temple tower beside Marduk's temple was rebuilt by Nebuchadnezzar II. A black stone stele in the Schøyen Collection shows Nebuchadnezzar beside the tower. Many scholars think towers like this lie in the background of the Babel story (Gen 11:1-9), though the Genesis narrative is set much earlier and the link is a matter of background, not identity.

Copies of the creation epic invited comparison with Gen 1, especially the dividing of the waters. Most scholars now see Genesis as answering the same questions very differently — no battle, no divine bodies, humans made in God's image rather than as slave labour — rather than borrowing directly.

renamed.explanation: Bel is not a disguise but the ordinary Akkadian title 'lord', cognate with Hebrew baal. Merodach is the Hebrew spelling of Marduk. Some scholars suggest the vowels of Merodach were shaped by the pattern of other deliberately altered names (like Molech), but there is no clear evidence of a shame-word here; it may simply reflect how the name was pronounced.

laterFate: Marduk's cult continued under the Persians and Greeks; Alexander the Great planned to rebuild the Esagila, and cuneiform temple records from Babylon run into the first century AD. As Babylon emptied, the god faded. In Jewish storytelling he survived as the idol unmasked by Daniel in the Greek addition *Bel and the Dragon*, where priests secretly eat the food offered to Bel. Some have suggested that the name Mordecai derives from Marduk; this is widely accepted as the etymology of the name but says nothing about Mordecai's own faith.

name: Nabu
original: Akkadian Nabû ('the one who calls' or 'the announcer'); Hebrew Nebo
symbol: A scribe's stylus or wedge, often shown standing on a mushhushshu dragon or on a clay tablet

cultCenter.name: Ezida temple, Borsippa (Birs Nimrud)

plain: Nabu was the Babylonian god of writing and wisdom, the patron of scribes, and the son of Marduk. In the Bible he is called Nebo. His name is hidden in some of the most famous names of the exile: Nebuchadnezzar and Nebuzaradan both begin with 'Nabu'.
myth:
Nabu had few long stories of his own. His importance lay in his job: he was the divine scribe who wrote on the 'tablet of destinies', recording each person's fate and the lifespan of kings. In the first millennium BC he became so popular that Assyrian and Babylonian kings named their sons after him. An Assyrian inscription on a Nabu statue from Kalhu (Nimrud) reads, roughly, 'trust in Nabu, do not trust in any other god'.

Every year at the New Year festival Nabu's statue was carried by boat from his temple at Borsippa to Babylon to visit his father Marduk, and then carried home again. If the festival could not be held, as happened during King Nabonidus's long absence in Arabia, the chronicles note that 'Nabu did not come to Babylon'.
biblicalRole:
Isaiah names Nebo alongside Bel as the two great gods of Babylon who end up as cargo: 'Bel bows down, Nebo stoops' (Isa 46:1). The image almost certainly plays on the procession in which Nabu was ferried to Babylon each year.

Nabu also appears in personal names connected with Judah's fall: Nebuchadnezzar (Nabu-kudurri-usur, 'Nabu, protect my heir'), his captain Nebuzaradan (Nabu-zer-iddin, 'Nabu has given offspring', 2 Kgs 25:8), and the officials Samgar-nebo and Nebushasban (Jer 39:3; Jer 39:13). Many scholars think Abednego's name (Dan 1:7) is a deliberate distortion of Abed-nebo ('servant of Nabu'), changing the god's name so it could not be honoured; others see it simply as an Aramaic form. This is debated.

A separate question is whether the Moabite town and mountain called Nebo (Num 32:3; Deut 34:1) were named after the god. Some scholars think a West Semitic form of the deity lies behind the place name; others think it is an unrelated word. Treat it as debated.

encounters.title: Nebo stoops
encounters.summary: The idol of the scribe-god, who supposedly wrote the destinies of nations, cannot save itself from being carried away.

encounters.title: Nabu's name on Judah's conquerors
encounters.summary: The Babylonians who besieged and burned Jerusalem carried Nabu's name. Jeremiah lists several of the officials who sat in the city's Middle Gate after it fell.

encounters.title: Abednego: a defaced name?
encounters.summary: Azariah was renamed Abednego. If the original was Abed-nebo, the book of Daniel may have scrambled the god's name, much as other biblical writers changed Baal names. This is a reasonable but unproven suggestion.

encounters.title: Mount Nebo and the town of Nebo
encounters.summary: Moses viewed the land from Mount Nebo. Num 32:38 notes that the Reubenites changed the names of some towns including Nebo, which may hint that the names had pagan associations. The Mesha Stele also mentions Mesha taking the town of Nebo from Israel.

archaeology.summary: This chronicle records year after year that because the king stayed in Tayma (Arabia), 'Nabu did not come to Babylon, Bel did not come out' and the New Year festival was not held. It confirms how central the Nabu-and-Bel procession was to Babylonian religion — the procession Isa 46 turns into a joke.

The ruined ziggurat of Borsippa, rebuilt by Nebuchadnezzar II, was long confused by travellers with the Tower of Babel. Inscribed cylinders of Nebuchadnezzar and Antiochus I describe rebuilding Nabu's temple.

A small business tablet dated 595 BC names Nabu-sharrussu-ukin, a chief eunuch of Nebuchadnezzar. Many scholars connect him with 'Sarsechim, Rab-saris' in Jer 39:3, though the exact reading of the Hebrew name list is debated.

renamed.explanation: One common suggestion is that a scribe changed b to g so that the name no longer honoured Nabu. Others think 'nego' is a genuine variant or an Aramaic form. The evidence is not decisive.

laterFate: Nabu was one of the last Mesopotamian gods to be worshipped. His cult spread to Syria, where he was honoured at Palmyra and Edessa into the Roman period, and Greek writers sometimes matched him with Apollo or Hermes as a god of learning. Borsippa's temple was still functioning in the Seleucid era.

name: Nergal
original: Sumerian/Akkadian Nergal (perhaps 'lord of the great city', i.e. the underworld)
domains: the scorching midday and summer sun
symbol: A lion-headed mace or curved sword (scimitar); the lion

cultCenter.name: E-meslam temple, Cuthah (Tell Ibrahim)

family.name: Enlil, chief god of Nippur (in most traditions)

plain: Nergal was the Mesopotamian god of plague, war and the land of the dead, and his chief city was Cuthah in central Iraq. When the Assyrians resettled people from Cuthah in the former kingdom of Israel, they brought Nergal with them. The Bible states this in a single sentence that matches the god to the right city.
myth:
In the myth *Nergal and Ereshkigal*, the gods hold a banquet and Ereshkigal, queen of the underworld, cannot come up to it, so she sends her messenger. Nergal fails to show proper respect and is summoned below. In one version he storms the underworld with demons and seizes the throne; in another, longer version he and Ereshkigal become lovers, and he ends up ruling the underworld with her. Either way, the story explains how a warrior god came to be king of the dead.

In the related *Erra Epic* (first millennium BC), the plague-and-war god Erra (identified with Nergal) persuades Marduk to leave his throne and then runs amok, devastating Babylon, until he is calmed. Copies of this poem were used as amulets against plague.
biblicalRole:
After Samaria fell (722 BC), the Assyrians deported many Israelites and brought in people from Babylon, Cuthah, Avva, Hamath and Sepharvaim (2 Kgs 17:24). Each group 'made its own gods': 'the men of Cuth made Nergal' (2 Kgs 17:30). The writer of Kings correctly pairs Cuthah with its patron god, which shows real knowledge of Mesopotamian religion.

The narrator's point is that these settlers 'feared the LORD and served their own gods' at the same time (2 Kgs 17:33; 2 Kgs 17:41) — a mixed religion. Later Jewish writers called the Samaritans 'Cutheans' (Kutim) after this verse, a hostile nickname implying that their worship was foreign in origin. Samaritans themselves reject that account of their origins.

Nergal's name also appears in Nergal-sharezer (Nergal-sharri-usur, 'Nergal, protect the king'), a Babylonian official present at the fall of Jerusalem (Jer 39:3; Jer 39:13). He is often identified with Neriglissar, who later became king of Babylon (560-556 BC); that identification is likely but not certain.

encounters.title: The men of Cuth make Nergal
encounters.summary: Settlers in Samaria set up Nergal's image in the old high places while also hiring an Israelite priest to teach them how to 'fear the LORD'.

encounters.title: Nergal-sharezer at the fall of Jerusalem
encounters.summary: A Babylonian commander bearing Nergal's name sits in the gate of conquered Jerusalem and later helps release Jeremiah.

archaeology.find: Nimrud Prism and Khorsabad annals of Sargon II
archaeology.summary: Sargon II claims he deported about 27,000 people from Samaria and resettled the city with people from other conquered lands, matching the policy described in 2 Kgs 17:24.
One of Sennacherib's city gates was named for Nergal and guarded by human-headed winged bulls. The bulls were badly damaged by militants in 2015.

laterFate: Nergal remained a feared god into Hellenistic and Parthian times; at Hatra and Palmyra he was matched with Heracles. Later Jewish tradition (b. Sanhedrin 63b) claimed the Cutheans' Nergal had the form of a rooster, a rabbinic guess based on a wordplay, not on Mesopotamian evidence. In medieval and early modern demonology Nergal became a minor demon, sometimes called a 'chief of secret police' in hell — a purely literary invention.

name: Ishtar
original: Akkadian Ištar; Sumerian Inanna ('Lady of Heaven')
symbol: An eight-pointed star (Venus), the lion, and the rosette

cultCenter.name: Eanna temple, Uruk (also Nineveh and Arbela)

family.name: Sin (Nanna), the moon, in many traditions

plain: Ishtar was the most important goddess of Mesopotamia: goddess of love, war and the morning and evening star (Venus). She is not named directly in the Bible, but many scholars think she stands behind the 'Queen of Heaven' whom the women of Judah honoured with cakes, and she is the lover of Tammuz, for whom women wept at the temple gate.
myth:
In the Sumerian *Descent of Inanna* (and the shorter Akkadian *Descent of Ishtar*), the goddess decides to visit the underworld, ruled by her sister. At each of seven gates she must give up one piece of clothing or jewellery, until she arrives naked and powerless and is struck dead and hung on a hook. With the help of the god of wisdom she is revived, but she may only leave if someone takes her place. She finds her lover Dumuzi enjoying himself instead of mourning, and hands him over to the demons. In a fragment published by Samuel Noah Kramer in 1963, Dumuzi's sister agrees to share his fate, so each spends half the year below.

Ishtar is also the dangerous goddess of the *Epic of Gilgamesh*, who proposes to Gilgamesh; when he refuses, listing the bad ends of her earlier lovers, she sends the Bull of Heaven to punish him. She was the battle goddess of Assyrian kings, who claimed she marched before their armies.
biblicalRole:
No biblical verse names Ishtar outright, so every link is inferred.

1. **The Queen of Heaven.** Jeremiah condemns families who make cakes, pour drink offerings and burn incense to 'the Queen of Heaven' (Jer 7:18; Jer 44:17-19). Ishtar bore titles like 'Lady of Heaven', and cakes were offered to her in Mesopotamian ritual; but Astarte and Anat were also called 'queen of heaven' in Egyptian and Levantine sources. Most scholars think the Judahite goddess was a blend in which Ishtar's influence (spread by Assyrian domination) mixed with the local Astarte. See the separate entry queen-of-heaven.

2. **Tammuz.** Ezekiel sees women 'weeping for Tammuz' at the north gate of the temple (Ezek 8:14). Tammuz is Ishtar's lover Dumuzi, so the rite belongs to her cycle.

3. **Nineveh as a seductive woman.** Nahum calls Nineveh 'the well-favoured harlot, the mistress of witchcrafts' (Nah 3:4). Some interpreters hear an allusion to Ishtar of Nineveh, the city's great goddess; this is plausible but not provable.

4. **Esther's name.** Esther's Persian name is often derived from Ishtar; others derive it from Persian *stara*, 'star'. Since Ishtar was the star goddess, the two ideas overlap. Debated.

encounters.title: Cakes for the Queen of Heaven
encounters.summary: Whole families in Judah, and later refugees in Egypt, honoured a goddess with cakes 'in her image'. The refugees told Jeremiah that things went well when they served her and badly when they stopped. Identification with Ishtar is likely in part, but debated.

encounters.title: Women weeping for Tammuz
encounters.summary: Ezekiel's vision of the temple shows women mourning Ishtar's dying lover — a rite from her mythology practised at the house of Yahweh.

encounters.title: The harlot of Nineveh
encounters.summary: Nahum's portrait of Nineveh as a seductive sorceress may borrow imagery from the city's goddess.

archaeology.summary: Nebuchadnezzar II's blue glazed-brick gate, dedicated to Ishtar, decorated with bulls and dragons, with a long inscription. It stood at the head of the Processional Way during the years when Judean exiles lived in Babylon.
Tablets of the descent myth show how the goddess and her lover were linked to death and return, the background to the Tammuz rite of Ezek 8.

archaeology.year: acquired by the British Museum 2003; known since 1930s
archaeology.summary: A clay plaque (c. 1800 BC) of a winged, bird-footed goddess with lions and owls. It is often popularly labelled 'Lilith', but most specialists identify her as Ishtar or her sister Ereshkigal.

renamed.explanation: Esth 2:7 says Hadassah was also called Esther. Many scholars derive Esther from Ishtar, as Mordecai is derived from Marduk; others prefer the Persian word for 'star'. This is not a hostile renaming but a court name.

laterFate: Ishtar's worship lasted in Mesopotamia into the Parthian period, and she merged with Aphrodite, Atargatis and other goddesses in the Greco-Roman East. Her descent myth has been widely studied as one of the earliest stories of death and return, though scholars now caution against the older idea of a single 'dying and rising god' pattern.

name: Sin (the moon god)
original: Akkadian Sîn (from Suen); Sumerian Nanna
symbol: A crescent moon, often a crescent on a pole with tassels; sometimes a bull with crescent horns

cultCenter.name: Ehulhul temple, Harran (also the Ekishnugal temple at Ur)

plain: Sin was the moon god of Mesopotamia. His two great temples were at Ur in the south and Harran in the north — the two cities where Abraham's family lived. The Bible never names Sin, but it remembers that Abraham's ancestors 'served other gods' and repeatedly forbids worship of the moon.
myth: Sin was the wise, slow-moving father of the bright gods: the sun (Shamash) and Venus (Ishtar). He sailed across the night sky in a boat shaped like the crescent moon. Because the moon marks out months, he was the keeper of the calendar and the god who decided the timing of things. In one story, an eclipse is explained as demons attacking Sin, and the gods have to rescue him. Shepherds and cattle-herders were especially devoted to him, and he was believed to give oracles in dreams.
biblicalRole:
Abraham's father Terah moved the family from 'Ur of the Chaldees' to Harran (Gen 11:31). Both cities were famous centres of the moon god, and Josh 24:2 says plainly that Terah and his family 'served other gods' beyond the River. Some scholars note that family names like Laban ('white', a poetic word for the moon in Hebrew is levanah) and Milcah and Sarah (which resemble Malkatu and Sharratu, titles of moon-related goddesses at Harran) may echo moon worship. These name links are speculative but often discussed.

The Law forbids worship of 'the sun, or the moon, or the stars, all the host of heaven' (Deut 4:19; Deut 17:3), and Job lists kissing one's hand to the moon as a secret disloyalty to God (Job 31:26-28). Josiah later removed priests who burned incense to the moon (2 Kgs 23:5). By contrast, Gen 1:16 refuses even to name the sun and moon, calling them only 'the greater light' and 'the lesser light' — lamps made by God, not gods.

The last king of Babylon, Nabonidus, was a passionate devotee of Sin, which angered Marduk's priests. His son Belshazzar governed Babylon in his absence — which explains why Belshazzar can only offer Daniel the third place in the kingdom (Dan 5:7; Dan 5:29).

encounters.title: Abraham's family leaves Ur for Harran
encounters.summary: The call of Abraham takes him out of two moon-god cities. Joshua's covenant speech later reminds Israel that its ancestors worshipped other gods there and calls them to choose (Josh 24:14-15).

encounters.title: Moon worship forbidden
encounters.summary: The sun, moon and stars are created things, not gods. Jeremiah pictures the bones of Jerusalem's leaders spread out before the sun and moon they served — the sky-gods watching, unable to help.

encounters.title: Josiah removes the moon priests
encounters.summary: Josiah's reform deposes the priests who burned incense 'to Baal, to the sun, and to the moon, and to the planets'.

encounters.title: Harran falls to Assyria
encounters.summary: Sennacherib's envoys boast that the gods of Harran could not save it from Assyria. Ezekiel later lists Harran as one of Tyre's trading partners.

encounters.title: Belshazzar, son of the moon-king
encounters.summary: Cuneiform texts show Belshazzar was regent for his father Nabonidus, who spent years in Arabia and promoted Sin; Daniel's 'third ruler' detail fits this arrangement.

archaeology.find: Harran stelae of Nabonidus and Adad-guppi
archaeology.place: Harran, south-east Turkey (reused as paving in the Great Mosque)
archaeology.summary: Inscriptions of Nabonidus and his mother Adad-guppi, a devotee of Sin who claimed to have lived over 100 years. They describe Sin's anger, the god's ten-year abandonment of Harran, and Nabonidus's rebuilding of the Ehulhul temple. They show the king's devotion to the moon god that so annoyed Babylon's priests.

Nabonidus prays to Sin for himself and for 'Belshazzar, my firstborn son'. This was one of the first texts to confirm Belshazzar as a historical figure, whom some nineteenth-century critics had doubted.

archaeology.find: Ziggurat and temple of Nanna at Ur
archaeology.summary: Woolley excavated the great moon-god ziggurat and residences of the high priestesses of Nanna, including those of Ennigaldi-Nanna, Nabonidus's daughter. Whether biblical 'Ur of the Chaldees' is this southern Ur or a northern site near Harran is debated, though southern Ur is the majority view.

archaeology.find: Moon-god stelae at Hazor and Bethsaida
archaeology.summary: A Late Bronze Age shrine at Hazor had a stele with two raised hands beneath a crescent; an Iron Age stele at Bethsaida's city gate shows a bull-headed figure with a crescent, a type found in Aram. They show moon worship in the land itself.

laterFate: Harran's moon cult outlived almost every other Mesopotamian religion. The Roman emperor Caracalla was murdered in AD 217 on his way to the moon temple; the emperor Julian sacrificed there in 363. Pagans of Harran, called 'Sabians' by Muslim writers, kept the cult alive until the eleventh century. The popular claim that Islam's crescent or Allah derives from the moon god Sin is not supported by historians: the crescent became an Islamic emblem only centuries later under Ottoman influence.

name: Sakkuth and Kaiwan
original: Akkadian Sakkut (SAG.KUD) and kayamānu ('the steady one', the planet Saturn); Hebrew Sikkut and Kiyyun
symbol: A star (the 'star of your god', Amos 5:26)

cultCenter.name: Mesopotamian astral cult (no single temple; shown at Babylon)

plain: Sakkuth and Kaiwan are two star-gods mentioned once by Amos, who accuses Israel of carrying their images. Kaiwan is the Mesopotamian name for the planet Saturn. Stephen quotes the same verse in Acts from the Greek translation, where the name has become 'Rephan'.
myth: There is no story about these gods. Kayamanu, 'the steady one', was the Babylonian name for Saturn, the slowest of the visible planets. Sakkut appears in Mesopotamian lists of gods and is connected with Ninurta, a warrior god, who was also linked to Saturn. In the Babylonian incantation series *Shurpu*, Sakkut and Kayamanu are listed side by side, which explains why Amos pairs them.
biblicalRole:
Amos asks whether Israel offered sacrifices in the wilderness, then says, 'You shall take up Sikkuth your king and Kiyyun your images, the star of your god, which you made for yourselves' (Amos 5:26, in a literal rendering). Older translations such as the KJV read the words as common nouns: 'the tabernacle (sukkat) of your Moloch and Chiun'. Modern scholars mostly read them as divine names because of the Mesopotamian pair.

A debate surrounds the verb tense: is Amos describing idolatry in the wilderness, idolatry in his own day (8th century BC, when Assyrian astral influence was growing), or what Israel will carry into exile (Amos 5:27)? Scholars differ.

Stephen quotes the passage in Acts 7:42-43 from the Septuagint: 'you took up the tent of Moloch and the star of your god Rephan'. The Greek translators read Hebrew *kiyyun* as something like *raiphan* — most likely an ancient copying confusion between similar letters, perhaps influenced by an Egyptian name for Saturn. Stephen uses the verse to argue that Israel's idolatry began in the wilderness right after the golden calf (Acts 7:41).

encounters.title: Amos: you carried your star-god
encounters.summary: Amos uses the star-gods to show that Israel's worship had been compromised, and threatens exile 'beyond Damascus'.

encounters.title: Stephen: the star of your god Rephan
encounters.summary: Stephen's speech links the golden calf, the host of heaven, Moloch and Rephan into one story of rejection, quoting the Greek text of Amos.

encounters.title: Worship of the host of heaven
encounters.summary: Kings records that both northern Israel and later Manasseh of Judah worshipped 'all the host of heaven', the wider astral religion to which Sakkuth and Kaiwan belong.

archaeology.year: edited by Erica Reiner, 1958 (tablets from Nineveh and elsewhere)
archaeology.place: Library of Ashurbanipal and other Mesopotamian archives
archaeology.summary: This exorcism series lists the gods Sakkut and Kayamanu next to each other, the same pairing found in Amos 5:26. This is the main reason scholars read Amos's words as divine names.
Records of planetary observations name Saturn as kayamanu, confirming the planetary meaning of Kaiwan.

renamed.explanation: The Hebrew vowels of both names (i-u) appear to copy the vowels of *shiqquts*, 'detestable thing', a word used for idols — the same scribal technique that turned Ashtart into Ashtoreth. The Greek form Rephan probably arose from misreading the Hebrew letters.

laterFate: The names vanished from worship but survive in Bible translations, where they have caused centuries of confusion. Because Acts 7:43 calls Rephan's symbol a 'star', some modern groups have claimed that the six-pointed Star of David derives from 'the star of Remphan'. Historians reject this: the hexagram became a Jewish emblem only in the Middle Ages and has no connection with Amos's star-god.

name: Nisroch
original: Hebrew Nisrok — identity uncertain (Nusku? Ninurta? Ashur? Marduk?)
domains: unknown — named only as the god in whose temple Sennacherib was killed
symbol: Unknown; the popular eagle-headed image is a nineteenth-century misidentification

cultCenter.name: Nineveh (temple named in 2 Kgs 19:37)

plain: Nisroch is the god in whose temple the Assyrian king Sennacherib was murdered by his own sons, after his failed siege of Jerusalem. No Assyrian god by this exact name is known, so scholars still argue over who he was. The murder itself is confirmed by Babylonian and Assyrian records.
myth: No myth survives because no god called Nisroch is attested outside the Bible. Proposed identifications include Nusku, the fire god and divine messenger, who had a temple at Nineveh; Ninurta, the warrior god; Ashur, the national god of Assyria (with the name garbled in copying); and Marduk. Each suggestion requires assuming that the Hebrew form has been altered, either accidentally or deliberately.
biblicalRole:
Kings and Isaiah tell the same story. Sennacherib besieged Jerusalem in 701 BC and mocked Hezekiah's trust in Yahweh. The angel of the LORD struck the Assyrian camp, and Sennacherib returned to Nineveh. 'And it came to pass, as he was worshipping in the house of Nisroch his god, that Adrammelech and Sharezer his sons smote him with the sword' (2 Kgs 19:37; Isa 37:38). His son Esarhaddon succeeded him.

The irony is deliberate. Sennacherib's envoys had asked, 'Has any of the gods of the nations delivered his land out of the hand of the king of Assyria?' (2 Kgs 18:33). In the end Sennacherib's own god could not protect him in his own temple. The narrative compresses time: the murder happened in 681 BC, twenty years after the siege, which the text does not hide but does not stress either.

encounters.title: Sennacherib killed in the house of Nisroch
encounters.summary: The king who mocked Israel's God is cut down by his sons while worshipping his own. Chronicles adds that he returned 'with shame of face'.

encounters.title: The boast that provoked it
encounters.summary: The Rabshakeh's speech lists the gods of Hamath, Arpad, Sepharvaim, Hena and Ivah, none of whom saved their people. The Nisroch scene answers this boast.

archaeology.year: acquired by the British Museum in the 1880s
archaeology.summary: The chronicle records that on the 20th of Tebet (681 BC) 'his son killed Sennacherib, king of Assyria, in a rebellion', confirming the biblical account of a son's murder of the king.

Esarhaddon describes how his brothers revolted, 'butting each other like young goats' for the kingship, and how he defeated them. In 1980 Simo Parpola argued from a letter that the murderer was Arda-Mulissu, which matches the biblical Adrammelech; this is widely accepted.

archaeology.find: Sennacherib's Prism (Taylor and Oriental Institute prisms)
archaeology.summary: Sennacherib's own account of the 701 BC campaign says he shut Hezekiah up in Jerusalem 'like a bird in a cage', received heavy tribute, but conspicuously does not claim to have taken the city.

renamed.explanation: Because the name is otherwise unknown, many scholars think it is a corrupted or deliberately distorted form of a known god's name. No consensus has emerged on which god.

laterFate: In 1849 Austen Henry Layard labelled the eagle-headed winged figures on Assyrian palace reliefs 'Nisroch', and the label stuck in popular books. Specialists now know those figures are apkallu, protective sages, not a god. Later demonologies made Nisroch a chief cook of hell, which is pure invention.

name: Adrammelech and Anammelech
original: Hebrew 'Adrammelek and 'Anammelek; perhaps Adad-milki ('Adad is king') and Anu-milki ('Anu is king'), or West Semitic forms
domains: child sacrifice by fire, according to 2 Kgs 17:31
symbol: Unknown

cultCenter.name: Sepharvaim (location uncertain; Sippar shown)

plain: Adrammelech and Anammelech were the gods of Sepharvaim, whose people were resettled in Samaria by the Assyrians. The Bible says these settlers burned their children in the fire to them. Where Sepharvaim was, and who exactly these gods were, is still debated.
myth: No myths survive. The names look like compounds with -melek ('king'). Adrammelech has been read as Adad-milki ('Adad is king', Adad being the storm god, the Mesopotamian Hadad) or as a West Semitic Adar-malik ('the glorious one is king'). Anammelech may contain Anu, the sky god, or Anat. Because child sacrifice is not well attested in Mesopotamia proper, some scholars think Sepharvaim was a Syrian town where Levantine molk-type rites were practised.
biblicalRole:
The list of settlers' gods ends: 'the Sepharvites burnt their children in fire to Adrammelech and Anammelech, the gods of Sepharvaim' (2 Kgs 17:31). The same city appears in the Assyrian boast — 'Where are the gods of Sepharvaim?' (2 Kgs 18:34; 2 Kgs 19:13). The writer of Kings uses these foreign gods to show how far the land had fallen: the territory of Israel, already condemned for passing children through the fire (2 Kgs 17:17), now hosts openly imported child sacrifice.

Confusingly, Adrammelech is also the name of one of Sennacherib's sons who murdered him (2 Kgs 19:37). The two are unrelated; the son's name has been matched with the Assyrian Arda-Mulissu.

**Where was Sepharvaim?** Options include Sippar in Babylonia (an old guess, now less favoured because the other places in the list are mostly Syrian), Sibraim between Damascus and Hamath (Ezek 47:16), or an otherwise unknown Syrian town. Debated.

encounters.title: Settlers burn children to the gods of Sepharvaim
encounters.summary: The narrator lists this among the practices of the new population of Samaria, who 'feared the LORD' while serving their own gods.

encounters.title: Where are the gods of Sepharvaim?
encounters.summary: Assyria's envoy cites Sepharvaim as a conquered city whose gods failed, to frighten Jerusalem into surrender.

encounters.title: Israel's own law against it
encounters.summary: The law forbids making children 'pass through the fire', so the Sepharvite rite is presented as the climax of everything Israel had been warned against.

archaeology.find: Sargon II's deportation records (Nimrud Prism, Khorsabad annals)
archaeology.summary: Assyrian texts describe moving conquered peoples into Samaria, the policy that brought the Sepharvites there. Sepharvaim itself has not been securely identified.

laterFate: The gods are known only from this passage. Milton placed Adramelec among the rebel angels in *Paradise Lost*, and later occult writers turned him into a demon of high rank — an invention with no ancient basis.

name: Succoth-benoth
original: Hebrew Sukkot benot ('booths of daughters') — probably a reshaped Babylonian divine name
domains: uncertain; if Sarpanitu, pregnancy and birth, and consort of Marduk
symbol: Unknown

cultCenter.name: Babylon (Esagila, if Sarpanitu)

plain: Succoth-benoth is the god or goddess that settlers from Babylon set up in Samaria. In Hebrew the name means 'booths of daughters', which sounds more like a place than a deity, so most scholars think it is a garbled or mocking form of a Babylonian name — most often Sarpanitu, Marduk's wife.
myth: If Succoth-benoth is Sarpanitu, she was the consort of Marduk, honoured alongside him in the Esagila temple, and associated with pregnancy and birth. A popular etymology linked her name to *zer-banitu*, 'creatress of seed', which may explain how Hebrew ears heard -benoth. Other suggestions are Marduk himself (via an epithet) or Banitu, 'creatress', a title of several goddesses.
biblicalRole:
'The men of Babylon made Succoth-benoth' (2 Kgs 17:30). Since every other group in the list makes a god, Succoth-benoth must be the deity of the Babylonian settlers, which points to Marduk or his consort.

An older interpretation, found in some nineteenth-century commentaries, took the Hebrew literally as 'booths of daughters' and connected it with Herodotus's story (*Histories* 1.199) of Babylonian women sitting in a temple precinct until a stranger paid for sex. Most modern scholars reject both the literal reading of the name and the reliability of Herodotus's account of 'sacred prostitution'.

encounters.title: The men of Babylon make Succoth-benoth
encounters.summary: The Babylonian settlers set up their own deity in Samaria's high places.

archaeology.summary: Royal inscriptions and temple rituals name Sarpanitu as Marduk's consort in the Esagila. These support, but do not prove, the identification with Succoth-benoth.

renamed.original: Probably Sarpanitu or Zarbanit (or another Babylonian divine title)
renamed.explanation: The Hebrew may reflect what a foreign name sounded like to Hebrew speakers, or a deliberate reshaping into a mildly mocking phrase. The exact mechanism is unknown.

laterFate: Known only from 2 Kgs 17:30. Milton does not list her, but some later demonologies made Succorbenoth a demon of jealousy, without any ancient basis.

name: Ashima
original: Hebrew 'Ashima'; possibly related to Aramaic Ashim / Eshem ('name') as in Eshem-Bethel
domains: uncertain; possibly a divine 'Name' or hypostasis
symbol: Unknown

cultCenter.name: Hamath (Hama), Syria

plain: Ashima was the god of the settlers from Hamath in Syria who were moved into Samaria. Almost nothing is known about this deity. The name may also lie behind Amos's phrase 'the sin of Samaria', and a similar divine name appears among the Jewish soldiers at Elephantine in Egypt.
myth: No myths survive. Hamath was an Aramean and Neo-Hittite city on the Orontes river, conquered by Assyria in 720 BC. The best extra-biblical parallel is the name Eshem-Bethel or Ashim-Bethel in a fifth-century BC list of temple contributions from Elephantine, which may mean 'the Name of Bethel' — a divine aspect worshipped alongside the god Bethel.
biblicalRole: 'The men of Hamath made Ashima' (2 Kgs 17:30). Amos, preaching decades earlier, condemns those 'who swear by the sin of Samaria' (Amos 8:14). The Hebrew for 'sin' is *ashmat*, and many scholars think Amos is punning on, or directly naming, a goddess Ashimah worshipped in Samaria; others take it simply as 'guilt' or as a reference to the calf at Bethel. If the first view is right, Ashima was in Samaria before the deportations, which complicates 2 Kgs 17:30. Debated.

encounters.title: The men of Hamath make Ashima
encounters.summary: Hamathite settlers bring their deity into the high places of the former northern kingdom.

encounters.title: Swearing by the guilt of Samaria
encounters.summary: Amos lists oaths by 'the sin of Samaria', 'your god, O Dan', and 'the way of Beersheba'. The first may be a pun on Ashima.

archaeology.summary: A fifth-century BC Aramaic list of donations for 'Yahu' also sets aside money for Eshem-Bethel and Anat-Bethel. It shows a Jewish colony honouring other divine names, and gives the closest known parallel to Ashima.
Excavations uncovered the Iron Age citadel of Hamath, destroyed by Sargon II in 720 BC, but no inscription naming Ashima.

renamed.biblical: Ashmat Shomron, 'the guilt of Samaria' (Amos 8:14), if a pun
renamed.explanation: Changing one sound turns the deity's name into the Hebrew word for 'guilt', a technique seen elsewhere in the Bible's treatment of foreign gods. The pun is plausible but not certain.

laterFate: Known only from these verses and the Elephantine parallel. The Talmud (b. Sanhedrin 63b) says Ashima had the form of a goat, a rabbinic tradition with no known ancient support.

name: Nibhaz and Tartak
original: Hebrew Nibhaz and Tartaq — origin unknown
symbol: Unknown (rabbinic tradition says Nibhaz was dog-shaped and Tartak donkey-shaped)

cultCenter.name: Samaria, where the Avvites set them up (Avva itself is unlocated)

plain: Nibhaz and Tartak were the gods of the Avvites, one of the groups Assyria resettled in Samaria. They are the least understood gods in the Bible: we do not know where Avva was or what these gods were like.
myth: No myths or inscriptions are known. Scholars have offered guesses: an Elamite origin (from south-west Iran), a link between Tartak and the Syrian goddess Atargatis, or an Aramaic origin. None has won general support.
biblicalRole: 'The Avvites made Nibhaz and Tartak' (2 Kgs 17:31). Avva is probably the same as Ivvah, one of the cities whose gods failed to stop Assyria (2 Kgs 18:34; 2 Kgs 19:13). The passage's point is cumulative: one group after another brings its own god into the land, while also learning to 'fear the LORD', so that 'unto this day' they do both (2 Kgs 17:41).

encounters.title: The Avvites make Nibhaz and Tartak
encounters.summary: The last of the imported gods in the list of settlers' deities.

encounters.title: Mixed worship 'unto this day'
encounters.summary: The narrator concludes that these nations feared the LORD and served their graven images at the same time, a pattern he condemns.

archaeology.summary: Assyrian royal inscriptions confirm the two-way deportations that brought foreign groups into Samaria. No text mentions Nibhaz or Tartak.

laterFate: Rabbinic tradition (b. Sanhedrin 63b) explains Nibhaz as a dog ('barker', from *nabah*) and Tartak as a donkey, guesses based on Hebrew wordplay. Medieval demonologies later made Nibhaz a demon. Nothing more is known.

name: Tammuz
original: Hebrew Tammuz, from Akkadian Duʾuzu / Sumerian Dumuzi ('faithful son')
symbol: The shepherd's crook and flocks; reed huts and sheepfolds

cultCenter.name: Uruk and Bad-tibira (southern Iraq); shown at Uruk

plain: Tammuz (Sumerian Dumuzi) was a shepherd god, the lover of the goddess Ishtar, who was taken down to the underworld. Each year women mourned his death in the summer heat. Ezekiel saw women of Jerusalem 'weeping for Tammuz' at the very gate of God's temple.
myth:
In the Sumerian love songs, the shepherd Dumuzi courts and marries the goddess Inanna. In the *Descent of Inanna*, Inanna returns from the underworld needing a substitute and, finding Dumuzi sitting on a throne instead of grieving for her, hands him over to the demons. In *Dumuzi's Dream* he flees and is caught. A fragment published by Samuel Noah Kramer in 1963 suggests that Dumuzi and his sister Geshtinanna divide the year, each spending half in the underworld.

The death of Dumuzi was lamented in ritual songs, and the fourth month of the Babylonian calendar (June-July) bore his name. Older scholarship (James Frazer's *The Golden Bough*) made him the model 'dying and rising god' of fertility; modern specialists stress that Dumuzi's return is barely described and that the 'dying and rising' category was over-generalised. Debated.
biblicalRole:
In a vision dated 592 BC, Ezekiel is taken to the temple and shown a series of 'abominations', each worse than the last. At the north gate he sees 'women weeping for Tammuz' (Ezek 8:14) — a public mourning rite for a foreign god held at Yahweh's house. Then, worse still, twenty-five men turn their backs to the temple to worship the sun (Ezek 8:16). The vision explains why the glory of God departs (Ezek 10:18-19).

Two other passages are sometimes linked to Tammuz or his western counterpart Adonis, but both links are debated: the 'pleasant plants' and 'strange slips' of Isa 17:10-11 (possibly the quick-sprouting 'gardens of Adonis'), and 'the desire of women' disregarded by the king of the north in Dan 11:37, which some read as Tammuz/Adonis and others as the hope of the Messiah or simply natural affection.

encounters.title: Women weeping for Tammuz
encounters.summary: Ezekiel's vision exposes a mourning rite for Ishtar's lover held at the north gate of the temple, part of a sequence of increasingly serious violations.

encounters.title: Gardens that wither
encounters.summary: Isaiah describes plantings that sprout quickly and then fail. Some scholars see the 'gardens of Adonis', small pots of fast-growing seeds used in mourning for the dying god. Debated.

encounters.title: The desire of women
encounters.summary: The arrogant king ignores 'the desire of women'. One reading takes this as Tammuz/Adonis, a god popular among women; others reject the link.

archaeology.summary: Tablets of the Descent of Inanna, Dumuzi's Dream and love songs show the myth behind the mourning rite. Kramer's 1963 publication of the ending revised earlier views of the story.
The Akkadian version ends with instructions for the rites of Dumuzi, including lamentation, which corresponds to what Ezekiel saw.

laterFate: The fourth month of the Jewish calendar is still called Tammuz, a name adopted from Babylonian usage during the exile. Jerome wrote that a grove of Tammuz-Adonis had been planted over the cave of Jesus' birth at Bethlehem (Jerome, *Letter* 58.3), which some historians accept and others treat cautiously. Syriac and Arabic writers mention Harranian women still mourning 'Ta'uz' in the Middle Ages. Milton includes 'Thammuz' among the fallen angels.

name: Ra
original: Egyptian Rꜥ ('sun')
symbol: The sun disc encircled by a cobra (uraeus); a falcon-headed man crowned with the disc; the obelisk

cultCenter.name: Heliopolis (biblical On, Beth-shemesh)

family.name: Hathor (and Sekhmet) as the Eye of Ra

plain: Ra was Egypt's sun god, believed to sail across the sky by day and through the underworld by night. Pharaohs called themselves 'son of Ra'. Joseph married the daughter of a priest of Ra's great city, On, and many readers see the plague of darkness as a blow aimed at Ra — a traditional reading that scholars debate.
myth: At Heliopolis the creator Atum (merged with Ra as Atum-Ra) rose on the first mound out of the waters of chaos and produced the other gods. Each day Ra crossed the sky in his 'day-boat'; each night he travelled through the twelve hours of the underworld in his 'night-boat', where the chaos-serpent Apophis tried to swallow him and had to be defeated so the sun could rise. In the *Destruction of Mankind* story, Ra, grown old, sends his Eye (as Hathor-Sekhmet) to punish rebellious humans and then has to trick her with red-dyed beer to stop the slaughter.
biblicalRole:
Ra is never named in the Hebrew Bible, but he is present in names and places.

- Joseph married Asenath, daughter of Potiphera, priest of On (Gen 41:45; Gen 41:50; Gen 46:20). Potiphera means 'the one whom Ra has given'. On is Heliopolis, the sun-god's city.
- The store-city Rameses (Exod 1:11) bears the name of Pharaoh Ramesses ('Ra has fashioned him').
- Jeremiah predicts that Nebuchadnezzar will 'break the pillars of Beth-shemesh' (house of the sun) in Egypt (Jer 43:13) — the obelisks of Heliopolis. Ezekiel mocks On by spelling it Aven, 'wickedness' (Ezek 30:17).

**The plagues.** God says the Passover judgement is 'against all the gods of Egypt' (Exod 12:12; Num 33:4). Many interpreters therefore read the ninth plague — three days of darkness that could be felt, while Israel had light (Exod 10:21-23) — as a direct humiliation of Ra. This pairing is traditional and widely taught, but the text itself does not name Ra, and Egyptian gods had overlapping roles, so scholars disagree on how far to press one-plague-one-god charts. Treat it as a reasonable but debated reading.

encounters.title: Joseph marries into the priesthood of On
encounters.summary: Pharaoh gives Joseph an Egyptian name and Asenath, daughter of the priest of the sun-city. The narrative notes this without comment; later Jewish writers (the romance *Joseph and Aseneth*) felt the need to tell of her conversion.

encounters.title: Darkness over Egypt (traditional link to Ra; debated)
encounters.summary: Three days of darkness fall on Egypt while the Israelites have light. Because Ra was the supreme sun god and Pharaoh his son, many read this as the clearest plague-against-a-god. The Bible's explicit claim is broader: judgement on 'all the gods of Egypt'.

encounters.title: Breaking the obelisks of the sun-city
encounters.summary: Jeremiah, taken to Egypt against his will, predicts Babylon will shatter the sacred pillars of Heliopolis. Ezekiel renames On as Aven, 'trouble/wickedness'.

encounters.title: Sun worship forbidden in Israel
encounters.summary: Israel is forbidden to bow to the sun. Josiah removes horses and chariots dedicated to the sun; Ezekiel sees men in the temple bowing eastward to the sun.

archaeology.year: standing since c. 1950 BC; site excavated repeatedly since the 19th century
archaeology.summary: The only obelisk still standing at Heliopolis, from the sun temple of Ra. Other Heliopolis obelisks were carried off in antiquity, including the pair now called Cleopatra's Needles in London and New York.

Large fragments of a royal statue found in the Heliopolis sun-temple area, first reported as Ramesses II and then identified as Psamtik I (7th century BC), showing royal investment in Ra's city during the period of Judah's late kings.

renamed.biblical: Aven ('wickedness') in Ezek 30:17; Beth-shemesh ('house of the sun') in Jer 43:13
renamed.explanation: Ezekiel changes the vowels of On to make 'Aven', the same word Hosea used to mock Bethel as Beth-aven, 'house of wickedness' (Hos 4:15). Jeremiah translates the city's meaning into Hebrew.

laterFate: Ra remained central throughout Egyptian history, merging with Amun and later identified by Greeks with Helios. Heliopolis declined after Alexandria was founded, and its stones were used to build medieval Cairo. Ra's name survives in pharaohs' names such as Ramesses and in the modern popularity of Egyptian sun imagery.

name: Osiris
original: Egyptian Wsjr (Usir)
domains: kingship passed from father to son
symbol: A mummified king with green or black skin, holding the crook and flail and wearing the white atef crown; the djed pillar (his backbone)

cultCenter.name: Abydos

plain: Osiris was Egypt's god of the dead: a murdered king who was brought back to life to rule the underworld and judge souls. Every dead Egyptian hoped to become 'an Osiris'. The Bible never mentions him, but Egypt's death culture forms the background to Joseph's embalming, and some scholars connect Pharaoh's 'heavy heart' with Osiris's judgement scale.
myth:
Osiris was a good king of Egypt. His jealous brother Seth killed him (in later versions, by trapping him in a chest and later cutting his body into pieces scattered across Egypt). Osiris's wife Isis searched for him, gathered and wrapped his body — the first mummy — and conceived their son Horus by the revived Osiris. Osiris then became king of the underworld, while Horus grew up to defeat Seth and take the throne of the living. Each living pharaoh was identified with Horus, and each dead pharaoh with Osiris.

In the *Book of the Dead* (New Kingdom, from about 1550 BC), the dead person's heart is weighed on a scale against the feather of Maat (truth) in the presence of Osiris. A heart heavy with wrongdoing is eaten by the monster Ammit; a light heart passes on to eternal life.
biblicalRole:
Osiris is not named in Scripture.

- **Embalming.** Joseph orders Egyptian physicians to embalm Jacob, which takes forty days, with seventy days of mourning (Gen 50:2-3), and Joseph himself is embalmed and placed in a coffin in Egypt (Gen 50:26). The text records this without endorsing Egyptian afterlife beliefs; Joseph asks that his bones be carried to Canaan (Gen 50:25; Exod 13:19).
- **Pharaoh's heavy heart.** Exodus often says Pharaoh's heart was 'heavy' (Hebrew *kabed*, Exod 7:14; Exod 8:15; Exod 9:7). Some Egyptologists and biblical scholars (for example John Currid) suggest an ironic allusion to the weighing of the heart: Pharaoh's heart is heavy, so he fails the very judgement Osiris was supposed to preside over. Others think *kabed* simply means stubborn. Debated.
- **Plagues.** Exod 12:12 announces judgement on 'all the gods of Egypt'. Popular charts link Osiris to the first plague (the Nile was sometimes called his outflow) or to the death of the firstborn (as lord of the dead). These pairings are traditional and debated; the text names no individual god.

encounters.title: Jacob and Joseph embalmed
encounters.summary: Israel's patriarchs receive Egyptian burial practices, yet Joseph's dying wish looks beyond Egypt to the promised land.

encounters.title: The heavy heart of Pharaoh (possible Osiris allusion; debated)
encounters.summary: The repeated language of a 'heavy' heart may play on Egyptian judgement imagery, ironically marking Pharaoh as condemned.

encounters.title: Judgement on all the gods of Egypt
encounters.summary: The death of the firstborn, including Pharaoh's heir (the living Horus), is presented as God's verdict on Egypt's divine order. Any specific Osiris link is interpretive.

archaeology.year: 1903 (identified by Margaret Murray under Flinders Petrie); cleared 1912-1914 (Naville)
archaeology.place: Abydos, behind the temple of Seti I
archaeology.summary: A sunken, island-like cenotaph representing the tomb of Osiris surrounded by water, built under Seti I (c. 1290 BC).
A Middle Kingdom official describes organising the annual Osiris festival, a procession re-enacting the god's death and restoration — one of the oldest descriptions of religious drama.

archaeology.find: Papyrus of Ani (Book of the Dead)
archaeology.summary: Beautifully painted scenes of the weighing of the heart before Osiris, the best-known illustration of Egyptian judgement after death.

laterFate: Under the Ptolemies, Osiris was fused with the Apis bull as Serapis, a Greek-looking god promoted to unite Greeks and Egyptians. Isis and Osiris-Serapis cults spread across the Roman Empire and competed with early Christianity. Some popular writers claim the Gospels copied the Osiris myth; most historians reject this, noting that Osiris is not raised to bodily life on earth but becomes king of the dead.

name: Hapi
otherNames: Father of the gods (title in Nile hymns)
original: Egyptian Ḥꜥpj ('inundation')
symbol: A plump man with a pot belly and drooping breasts, crowned with papyrus or lotus plants, carrying offering tables of food

cultCenter.name: First Cataract region, Elephantine/Aswan (believed source of the flood); also Gebel el-Silsila

plain: Hapi was the god of the Nile's yearly flood, which fertilised Egypt's fields and made the country rich. He was not 'the river' itself so much as the life-giving inundation. The first plague, turning the Nile to blood, is traditionally read as a blow against Hapi and the Nile's sacred status — a link the text implies only in general terms.
myth: Hapi had almost no myths; he was praised rather than narrated. The Middle Kingdom *Hymn to the Nile* (Hymn to Hapi) thanks him for bringing food, making the barley and emmer grow, and filling the granaries, and warns that if he is slow, people starve. He was imagined as living in a cave near the First Cataract at Aswan, pouring the flood from jars. Hapi should not be confused with Apis (Egyptian Hep), the sacred bull.
biblicalRole:
Egypt's dependence on the Nile flood is a theme across the Bible. Moses tells Israel that the promised land is 'not as the land of Egypt', watered by foot-powered irrigation, but a land that 'drinks water of the rain of heaven' (Deut 11:10-11) — a land dependent on God rather than on a river.

**First plague.** Moses strikes the Nile, its water turns to blood, the fish die and the Egyptians cannot drink (Exod 7:14-25). Because the Nile and its flood were divine gifts embodied in Hapi (and associated with Osiris), the plague is widely read as an attack on Egypt's source of life and on its gods. The pairing is traditional and plausible, but the text names no Egyptian god, so it should be presented as interpretation (Exod 12:12; Num 33:4).

Ezekiel later calls Pharaoh 'the great dragon that lies in the midst of his rivers, which has said, My river is my own, and I have made it' (Ezek 29:3) — the claim to own and create the Nile is what God condemns. Isaiah's oracle on Egypt predicts the Nile drying up and fishermen mourning (Isa 19:5-8).

encounters.title: The Nile turned to blood (traditional link to Hapi; debated)
encounters.summary: The first plague strikes the river on which all Egyptian life depended. Interpreters link it to Hapi, Osiris or the Nile's divine status in general.

encounters.title: Not a land like Egypt
encounters.summary: Israel's new land will depend on rain from God, not on a predictable river — a theological contrast with Egypt's flood-god.

encounters.title: Pharaoh claims to have made the Nile
encounters.summary: The prophets judge Egypt's boast that the river belongs to Pharaoh, predicting its failure.

archaeology.find: Hymn to the Nile (Hymn to Hapi)
archaeology.year: copies in papyri acquired in the 19th century (e.g. Papyrus Sallier II, Anastasi VII)
archaeology.summary: A Middle Kingdom hymn praising the flood as the giver of all food. It shows how completely Egypt's life was tied to the Nile — the background to the first plague.

A Ptolemaic-era inscription telling of seven years of low Nile floods and famine under the ancient king Djoser, ended by honouring the god Khnum of the cataract. It is often compared with Joseph's seven years of famine (Gen 41:25-36), though it is much later and legendary.

archaeology.year: in use from antiquity; studied since the 19th century
archaeology.summary: A staircase gauge used to measure the height of the flood, on which taxes depended.

laterFate: Hapi continued to be depicted on temple walls into Roman times. The Nile flood stopped being annual after the Aswan High Dam was completed in 1970.

name: Heqet
original: Egyptian Ḥqt
symbol: A frog, or a woman with a frog's head

cultCenter.name: Her-wer, Middle Egypt (approximate; exact site not securely located)

family.name: Khnum, the ram-headed potter god who shaped bodies on his wheel

plain: Heqet was an Egyptian goddess shown as a frog, who helped women in childbirth and was linked with the breath of new life. Frogs swarmed from the Nile each year after the flood, so they symbolised abundance. The plague of frogs is often read as a mockery of Heqet, but this is a traditional, debated link.
myth: Heqet had few stories. In some traditions she gave the breath of life to the bodies her husband Khnum shaped on his potter's wheel. In the Westcar Papyrus story of the birth of three kings, Heqet is one of the goddesses who come disguised as midwives and 'hasten the birth'. Women wore frog amulets and used ivory birthing wands decorated with frogs and other protective figures. Because frogs appeared in huge numbers after the flood, the frog also became a hieroglyph for the number 100,000.
biblicalRole:
Heqet is not named in the Bible.

**Second plague.** At Moses' word, frogs come up from the Nile and fill houses, bedrooms, beds, ovens and kneading bowls (Exod 8:1-15). When they die they are piled in heaps and the land stinks. Pharaoh's magicians can produce more frogs but cannot remove them, and Pharaoh has to ask Moses to pray. Many interpreters see a deliberate mockery of a goddess of fertility and life: the symbol of blessing becomes a smothering nuisance and then a stinking ruin. This is a traditional reading; the text itself makes no mention of Heqet, and frogs were associated with other deities too. Treat as debated.

There is also a possible irony that some readers point out: the Egyptian goddess of midwives is overshadowed by the Hebrew midwives Shiphrah and Puah, who fear God and preserve Israel's babies (Exod 1:15-21). This link is speculative.

In Revelation, unclean spirits 'like frogs' come out of the mouths of the dragon, beast and false prophet (Rev 16:13) — perhaps an echo of the Exodus plague.

encounters.title: Frogs over the land (traditional link to Heqet; debated)
encounters.summary: A creature associated with fertility and blessing becomes a plague. Pharaoh is made to ask that the frogs be removed 'that you may know there is none like the LORD our God' (Exod 8:10).

encounters.title: Frog-like spirits
encounters.summary: Revelation's frog-like demonic spirits gather kings for battle, probably drawing on the Exodus plague imagery.

archaeology.find: Ivory apotropaic 'birth wands' and frog amulets
archaeology.year: excavated at many sites since the 19th century
archaeology.place: Middle Kingdom tombs and towns across Egypt
archaeology.summary: Curved ivory wands carved with protective beings including frogs, used to protect mothers and newborns, show Heqet's role in everyday religion.
A collection of tales including the birth of three kings attended by Isis, Nephthys, Meskhenet and Heqet disguised as midwives.

laterFate: Frog amulets remained popular in Egypt into the Roman era, and early Egyptian Christians used frog-shaped lamps, some with inscriptions such as 'I am the resurrection', reinterpreting the frog as a symbol of new life.

name: Apis
otherNames: Hapi (not to be confused with the Nile god)
original: Egyptian Ḥp
domains: the living 'herald' of the god Ptah
symbol: A black bull with a white triangle on its forehead and a sun disc between its horns

cultCenter.name: Memphis (temple of Ptah); burials at the Serapeum, Saqqara

plain: Apis was a real, living bull kept at Memphis and worshipped as the earthly form of the god Ptah. When an Apis bull died it was mummified and buried in a giant stone coffin, and priests searched Egypt for its successor. Some scholars see Apis behind the golden calf, and the Greek Bible explicitly names Apis in Jeremiah.
myth: Apis was chosen by markings: a black bull with a white triangle on the forehead, a vulture- or eagle-shaped patch on the back and other signs. Its mother was said to have been impregnated by a flash of light from heaven. The bull lived in a special enclosure at Memphis, gave oracles by its movements, and appeared in festivals. On death it became one with Osiris (Osiris-Apis), and in the Ptolemaic period this fused god became Serapis, worshipped across the Mediterranean.
biblicalRole:
Apis is not named in the Hebrew Bible, but there are three points of contact.

1. **The fifth plague.** A severe pestilence kills Egypt's livestock, including cattle, while Israel's animals are spared (Exod 9:1-7). In a culture that venerated sacred bulls and cows, this is often read as judgement on Apis and the cow goddess Hathor. Traditional; the text names no god (Exod 12:12; Num 33:4). Debated.

2. **The golden calf.** Some interpreters think Israel, fresh from Egypt, modelled the calf (Exod 32:4) on Apis. Others point out that a young bull was also the standard Levantine symbol for El and Baal, and that Aaron proclaimed a 'feast to the LORD' (Exod 32:5), suggesting an image of Yahweh or a pedestal for him rather than an Egyptian god. Debated; see golden-calf.

3. **Jeremiah 46:15 in Greek.** The Hebrew reads 'Why are your mighty ones (or: your mighty one) swept away?' The Septuagint divides the Hebrew letters differently and translates, 'Why has Apis fled? Your chosen calf did not stand.' Most scholars think the Greek translators preserved a genuine reference to Apis, which the later Hebrew text obscured.

encounters.title: Cattle struck by pestilence (traditional link to Apis and Hathor; debated)
encounters.summary: Egypt's livestock die while Israel's survive, a blow often read as aimed at Egypt's sacred cattle.

encounters.title: Why has Apis fled?
encounters.summary: In the Greek translation, Jeremiah's oracle on Egypt mocks the flight of the Apis bull before Nebuchadnezzar.

encounters.title: A calf at Sinai
encounters.summary: Stephen says that the Israelites 'turned back in their hearts to Egypt' and made a calf. Whether the calf imitated Apis is debated.

archaeology.summary: Long underground galleries hold twenty-four enormous granite and basalt sarcophagi, most from the Late Period. Inscribed Apis stelae dating the bulls' births and deaths have helped Egyptologists fix the reigns of pharaohs.

Herodotus (*Histories* 3.27-29) claims the Persian king Cambyses stabbed the Apis bull. A Serapeum epitaph shows an Apis buried with royal honours under Cambyses, so many historians doubt Herodotus's story.
The decree of Ptolemy V praises the king for generous gifts to the Apis and Mnevis bulls, showing the sacred bulls' importance into the second century BC.

renamed.original: Hebrew nsḥp ('swept away') read as ns ḥp ('Hap has fled')
renamed.explanation: The same consonants can be divided into different words. The Greek translators read a mention of Apis (Hep). Many scholars think this was the original sense.

laterFate: Through Serapis, the Apis cult outlived pharaonic Egypt. The Serapeum of Alexandria became one of the great temples of the Roman world until its destruction in AD 391 under the bishop Theophilus — a turning point in the end of paganism in Egypt.

name: Hathor
original: Egyptian Ḥwt-Ḥr
symbol: A cow, or a woman with cow ears or horns holding a sun disc; the sistrum (a sacred rattle)

cultCenter.name: Dendera

plain: Hathor was a much-loved Egyptian goddess of love, music, motherhood and joy, often shown as a cow. She was also the 'Lady of Turquoise' at the Egyptian mines in Sinai. Some interpreters connect her with the golden calf and with the plague on Egypt's cattle; both links are debated.
myth: Hathor was the 'Eye of Ra'. In the *Destruction of Mankind*, Ra sends her out to punish rebellious humans; she becomes the raging lioness Sekhmet and begins to slaughter them. To stop her, Ra floods the fields with beer dyed red to look like blood; she drinks it, becomes drunk and gentle, and returns as loving Hathor. Festivals of drunkenness re-enacted this. As the celestial cow she was also pictured as the sky itself and as the nurse of the king.
biblicalRole:
Hathor is not named in the Bible.

- **Sinai.** Egyptians mined turquoise at Serabit el-Khadim in south-western Sinai and built a large temple there to Hathor. Workers from Canaan left inscriptions in the earliest known alphabet, several addressed to Baalat, 'the Lady' — almost certainly Hathor. The location of biblical Mount Sinai is itself debated, but the region was not religiously empty when Israel passed through it.
- **The golden calf.** Some scholars suggest the calf at Sinai drew on Hathor's cow imagery as well as Apis's bull. The Hebrew word *egel* means a young bull, which fits Levantine bull iconography better. Debated.
- **Fifth plague.** As a cow goddess, Hathor is often listed in charts as a target of the plague on livestock (Exod 9:1-7). This pairing is traditional and debated (Exod 12:12; Num 33:4).

encounters.title: Livestock struck (traditional link to Hathor; debated)
encounters.summary: The death of Egypt's cattle is often read as aimed at the cow goddess and the bull Apis.

encounters.title: Revelry before the calf
encounters.summary: The people eat, drink and 'rise up to play', with singing and dancing around the calf. Some compare the scene with Hathor's music-and-drink festivals; most see generic festival language.

archaeology.find: Temple of Hathor and Proto-Sinaitic inscriptions
archaeology.year: 1904-1905 (Flinders Petrie); partly deciphered by Alan Gardiner, 1916
archaeology.summary: Short inscriptions in the earliest known alphabet, carved by Semitic-speaking workers (c. 1800-1500 BC), include l-bʿlt, 'to the Lady', addressed to Hathor. The alphabet that later produced Hebrew writing was born in a Hathor sanctuary.

An Egyptian mining shrine to Hathor was later taken over and remodelled, probably by Midianites, who defaced Hathor's images and set up a tent shrine with a copper snake — an intriguing parallel to Nehushtan.

archaeology.year: standing; cleared by Mariette in the 1850s
archaeology.summary: A well-preserved temple of Ptolemaic and Roman date, with the famous Dendera zodiac ceiling.

laterFate: Hathor's worship continued into Roman times, when Greeks identified her with Aphrodite. Her cow-ear face decorates columns across Egypt, many later defaced by Christians who saw the temples as homes of demons.

name: Amun
original: Egyptian Jmn ('the hidden one')
symbol: A man wearing a crown of two tall plumes; the ram with curved horns; the goose

cultCenter.name: Karnak temple, Thebes (biblical No / No-Amon)

plain: Amun, 'the hidden one', was the god of Thebes who became king of the Egyptian gods during Egypt's empire. His vast temple at Karnak was one of the largest religious complexes ever built. Jeremiah names him directly — 'Amon of No' — and Nahum reminds Nineveh how Amun's city of Thebes fell.
myth: Amun was invisible and present everywhere, the hidden breath behind all things. When Theban kings drove out the Hyksos (c. 1550 BC) and built an empire, they credited Amun, merged him with the sun god as Amun-Ra, and showered his temple with plunder from Canaan and Nubia. The Amun priesthood became immensely rich. Pharaoh Akhenaten briefly suppressed Amun in favour of the sun disc Aten (c. 1350 BC), but Amun was restored under Tutankhamun ('living image of Amun').
biblicalRole:
Jeremiah's oracle against Egypt announces: 'Behold, I will punish Amon of No, and Pharaoh, and Egypt, with their gods and their kings' (Jer 46:25). The KJV translates *Amon mi-No* as 'the multitude of No', but modern translations recognise the god's name.

Nahum warns Nineveh: 'Are you better than No-Amon (populous No), that was situated among the rivers?' — yet she was carried into captivity and her infants dashed to pieces (Nah 3:8-10). This refers to the Assyrian sack of Thebes in 663 BC, which Nineveh itself had carried out. Ezekiel also predicts judgement on No (Ezek 30:14-16).

Amun's temple also records Israel's history from the Egyptian side: Shoshenq I, almost certainly the biblical Shishak, celebrated his campaign into Judah and Israel on a wall at Karnak (cf. 1 Kgs 14:25-26).

encounters.title: I will punish Amon of No
encounters.summary: Jeremiah names Egypt's imperial god alongside Pharaoh as the target of judgement through Nebuchadnezzar.

encounters.title: Remember the fall of Thebes
encounters.summary: The prophets use Thebes, Amun's great city, as proof that no empire is safe.

encounters.title: Shishak plunders Jerusalem
encounters.summary: In Rehoboam's fifth year the pharaoh Shishak took the temple treasures of Jerusalem. Egyptian kings dedicated such spoils to Amun.

encounters.title: Plagues and the gods of Egypt
encounters.summary: Amun is sometimes included in plague charts, usually with Ra for the darkness. The Bible's claim is general: judgement on all Egypt's gods. Specific pairings are traditional and debated.

archaeology.summary: A relief shows Amun leading rows of captive towns to the pharaoh, with names that include places in Israel and the Negev. Most scholars connect it with Shishak's campaign (c. 925 BC), though Jerusalem is not clearly named and how the list relates to 1 Kgs 14 is debated.
Ashurbanipal boasts of capturing Thebes and carrying off its treasures and two obelisks (663 BC), the event Nahum 3:8-10 recalls.
Over two thousand years of building for Amun, including the great hypostyle hall of 134 columns.

renamed.explanation: The Hebrew Amon is very close to hamon, 'multitude', and older translations took it that way. Modern scholars agree the god is meant; whether a pun is intended is unclear.

laterFate: Greeks identified Amun with Zeus. Alexander the Great visited Amun's oracle at Siwa in 331 BC and was hailed as son of Zeus-Ammon, afterwards portrayed with ram's horns. The ancient name survives in the word 'ammonia', from salts collected near the Siwa temple.

name: Zeus
original: Greek Zeus (Διός in the genitive)
symbol: The thunderbolt, the eagle, the oak, and the royal sceptre

cultCenter.name: Temple of Zeus 'before the city', Lystra (Acts 14:13); chief Greek sanctuaries at Olympia and Dodona

family.relation: sons (Pollux in all versions; Castor in some)
family.name: Castor and Pollux, the Dioscuri

plain: Zeus was the king of the Greek gods, ruler of the sky and the thunderbolt; the Romans called him Jupiter. In Acts, the people of Lystra think Barnabas is Zeus and Paul is Hermes come down in human form, and the priest of Zeus tries to sacrifice oxen to them. Paul and Barnabas tear their clothes and insist they are only human.
myth:
Zeus was the youngest son of the Titan Cronus, who swallowed his children for fear of being overthrown. Zeus's mother hid him in Crete, and he later forced Cronus to vomit up his siblings, defeated the Titans and divided the world: Zeus took the sky, Poseidon the sea, Hades the underworld. He ruled from Mount Olympus. His many affairs with goddesses and mortal women produced gods and heroes.

One story matters especially for Acts. The Roman poet Ovid (*Metamorphoses* 8.611-724) tells how Jupiter and Mercury (Zeus and Hermes) once visited the hill country of Phrygia disguised as travellers. Everyone turned them away except an old couple, Baucis and Philemon, who were rewarded while their neighbours were destroyed by a flood. Many commentators think a local version of this legend explains why the Lystrans were so quick to honour Paul and Barnabas: they did not want to make the same mistake twice.
biblicalRole:
**Lystra.** After Paul heals a man lame from birth, the crowd shouts in Lycaonian, 'The gods have come down to us in the likeness of men!' They call Barnabas Zeus and Paul Hermes, 'because he was the chief speaker'. The priest of Zeus, whose temple stood in front of the city, brings oxen and garlands to the gates (Acts 14:8-13). Paul answers with the first recorded sermon to pure pagans in Acts: turn from 'these vain things' to the living God who made heaven and earth and has shown his goodness through rain and harvests (Acts 14:15-17) — taking for the true God the very gifts Zeus was credited with.

**Ephesus.** The town clerk calls the Artemis statue 'the image which fell down from Jupiter' (Acts 19:35), literally 'fallen from Zeus' or 'from the sky' — probably a meteorite or an object believed to have fallen from heaven.

**Zeus in the temple.** In 167 BC the Seleucid king Antiochus IV rededicated the Jerusalem temple to Zeus Olympios (1 and 2 Maccabees describe this). Many interpreters see this as the 'abomination that makes desolate' of Dan 11:31 and Dan 12:11, which Jesus reapplies to a future crisis (Matt 24:15). The Maccabean link is the majority scholarly view; some conservative readers see Daniel pointing beyond it as well.

**Pergamum.** Jesus tells the church at Pergamum that they live 'where Satan's throne is' (Rev 2:13). The huge Altar of Zeus there is one candidate; others are the imperial cult temple or the healing sanctuary of Asclepius. Debated.

encounters.title: Barnabas hailed as Zeus at Lystra
encounters.summary: A crowd tries to sacrifice to the apostles as Zeus and Hermes. Paul and Barnabas tear their clothes and preach the Creator who gives rain and food. They barely restrain the crowd.

encounters.title: The image fallen from Zeus
encounters.summary: Ephesus's town clerk appeals to the sacred image of Artemis, said to have fallen from the sky (from Zeus), to calm the riot.

encounters.title: The abomination of desolation
encounters.summary: Daniel's vision is widely read as describing Antiochus IV's altar to Zeus Olympios in the temple; Jesus reuses the phrase for a coming desecration.

encounters.title: Satan's throne at Pergamum
encounters.summary: Pergamum's great Altar of Zeus is one possible referent of 'Satan's throne'; scholars also propose the emperor cult or Asclepius. Debated.

archaeology.find: Inscriptions to Zeus and Hermes near Lystra
archaeology.place: Sedasa and nearby villages, Lycaonia (central Turkey)
archaeology.summary: Calder published a third-century AD dedication by men with Lycaonian names of a statue of Hermes to Zeus, and an altar to Zeus 'hearer of prayer' and Hermes. They show Zeus and Hermes were honoured together in this very region, which fits Acts 14. They are later than Paul, so they illustrate local religion rather than proving a particular temple.

archaeology.find: Lystra city site and Latin inscription naming the colony
archaeology.summary: An altar inscription naming the Roman colony of Lustra identified the site of the city. The temple of Zeus mentioned in Acts has not been found.
A monumental altar of the second century BC carved with the battle of gods and giants. It is one of the proposed referents of 'Satan's throne' in Rev 2:13.

renamed.explanation: The King James translators used the Latin names familiar from Roman literature. The Greek text has Zeus and Hermes.

laterFate: Zeus's public cult was progressively closed down by Christian emperors in the late fourth century, and the Olympic Games ended around AD 393. Christian writers saw in Paul's speech at Lystra the pattern for reaching pagans: start with creation and providence. Zeus survives in literature, art, astronomy (the planet Jupiter) and in the word 'Thursday' indirectly, via the Roman matching of Jupiter with Thor.

name: Hermes
original: Greek Hermēs
domains: guiding the souls of the dead
symbol: The caduceus (a herald's staff with two snakes), winged sandals and a traveller's hat

cultCenter.name: Mount Cyllene, Arcadia (his mythical birthplace)

plain: Hermes was the Greek messenger god, patron of speech, travel, merchants and tricksters; the Romans called him Mercury. At Lystra the crowd called Paul 'Hermes' because he did most of the talking. One of the Christians Paul greets in Rome is also named Hermes, a common name.
myth: Born in a cave on Mount Cyllene, the baby Hermes crept out on his first day, invented the lyre from a tortoise shell, and stole fifty cattle from his brother Apollo, walking them backwards to confuse the trail. Zeus was amused and made him the herald of the gods. He guided travellers and also led the souls of the dead to Hades. Square pillars with his head and phallus, called herms, stood at crossroads and doorways. As 'Hermes Logios' he was the god of eloquence — which is exactly why the Lystrans gave Paul his name.
biblicalRole:
At Lystra the crowd calls Barnabas Zeus and Paul Hermes 'because he was the chief speaker' (Acts 14:12). The detail shows the crowd's logic: the quieter, perhaps more dignified Barnabas was cast as the chief god, and the talkative Paul as his spokesman. Paul refuses the honour and urges them to turn from these 'vain things' to the living God (Acts 14:15).

In Rom 16:14, Paul greets a believer named Hermes. Names derived from gods were normal in the Roman world and carried no religious meaning in themselves.

encounters.title: Paul called Hermes
encounters.summary: Because Paul did the preaching, the people of Lystra identified him with the gods' messenger. Within days, opponents from Antioch and Iconium turned the same crowd to stone him (Acts 14:19).

encounters.title: A Christian named Hermes
encounters.summary: Among Paul's greetings is a believer called Hermes, a reminder that pagan names were simply names.

archaeology.find: Dedication of a statue of Hermes to Zeus
