archaeology.summary: Local men dedicated a statue of 'Hermes Megistos' and a sundial to Zeus. The inscription is later than Paul (third century AD) but shows the two gods paired in this part of Lycaonia.

renamed.explanation: The KJV used the Latin name; modern translations use Hermes as in the Greek.

laterFate: In late antiquity Hermes was merged with the Egyptian Thoth as 'Hermes Trismegistus', the supposed author of mystical writings (the Hermetica) that influenced Renaissance thought. The caduceus is still (inaccurately) used as a medical symbol, a confusion with the single-snake rod of Asclepius.

name: Artemis of the Ephesians
original: Greek Artemis
domains: fertility and nature (in her Ephesian form)
banking and asylum (her temple held deposits and gave refuge)
symbol: A rigid standing statue with many rounded objects on her chest, a tall crown shaped like a city wall, and animals carved on her lower body

cultCenter.name: The Artemision (Temple of Artemis), Ephesus

plain: Artemis was the great goddess of Ephesus, and her temple there was one of the Seven Wonders of the ancient world. The Ephesian Artemis was not quite the slim huntress of Greek myth but an older Anatolian mother-goddess. When Paul's preaching hurt the trade in silver shrines, a silversmith named Demetrius started a riot in which a crowd chanted 'Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!' for two hours.
myth:
In standard Greek myth, Artemis was the virgin huntress, daughter of Zeus and Leto and twin of Apollo, goddess of wild places and of childbirth. The Ephesians claimed she had actually been born near their city, in the grove of Ortygia. Their Artemis blended the Greek goddess with an older Anatolian goddess, which explains her distinctive statue. The many rounded objects on her chest have been explained as breasts, eggs, bull testicles from sacrifices, or decorative pendants; scholars still debate this.

The temple was rebuilt several times. Herostratus burned it in 356 BC, reportedly to make himself famous, on the night Alexander the Great was said to have been born. The rebuilt temple, about four times the size of the Parthenon, was the one Paul knew.
biblicalRole:
Paul spent about two to three years in Ephesus (Acts 19:8-10; Acts 20:31), and so many people abandoned magic that they burned scrolls worth fifty thousand pieces of silver (Acts 19:19). Demetrius, a silversmith who made silver shrines of Artemis, gathered the craftsmen: Paul's message that 'gods made with hands are not gods' threatened both their income and the goddess's honour (Acts 19:24-27). The crowd rushed into the theatre shouting 'Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!' for about two hours (Acts 19:28-34). The town clerk calmed them by reminding them that Ephesus was the 'temple-keeper' (neokoros) of Artemis, that Paul's companions had neither robbed temples nor blasphemed the goddess, and that the courts were open (Acts 19:35-40).

Some scholars also read parts of 1 Timothy, written to Timothy in Ephesus, against the background of the Artemis cult, especially the reference to women being 'saved through childbearing' (1 Tim 2:15), since Artemis was the protector in childbirth. This is a minority but much-discussed reading; others see no specific link.

encounters.title: The riot of the silversmiths
encounters.summary: An economic and religious protest fills the great theatre of Ephesus. Luke presents it as proof of the gospel's impact: the trade in shrines was suffering.

encounters.title: Magic books burned
encounters.summary: Ephesus was famous for magic ('Ephesian letters' were protective spells). New believers burn their scrolls publicly.

encounters.title: Artemis behind 1 Timothy? (debated)
encounters.summary: Some read the instructions about women and childbirth against the local goddess cult; others think the letter addresses general false teaching. See the gender-roles debate.

archaeology.year: 1869 (John Turtle Wood); 1904-1905 (D. G. Hogarth); Austrian excavations since 1965
archaeology.summary: After six years of searching, Wood found the temple's foundations under deep silt. Only one re-erected column now stands. Hogarth found early foundation deposits including some of the earliest coins ever made.
Two marble copies of the cult statue ('Great Artemis' and 'Beautiful Artemis'), carefully buried in antiquity, show the goddess's distinctive form.

A long inscription of AD 104 records a rich Roman's gift of gold and silver images of Artemis carried in procession between the temple and the theatre, illustrating the trade in sacred images Demetrius defended.
A theatre seating roughly 20,000-25,000 people, where the riot of Acts 19:29 took place.

renamed.explanation: The KJV used the Latin name of the Roman goddess identified with Artemis. Modern translations follow the Greek.

laterFate: The temple was damaged by Gothic raiders in AD 262 and fell into ruin as Christianity spread; an Ephesian inscription records a Christian replacing an image of Artemis with a cross. Stones from the temple were reused in later buildings, including, according to tradition, Hagia Sophia in Constantinople (debated). Ephesus later hosted the Council of Ephesus (431), which honoured Mary as Theotokos; some writers claim Marian devotion simply replaced Artemis, but historians see a far more complex history.

name: Castor and Pollux
original: Greek Dioskouroi
symbol: Twin young men with star-topped caps (piloi) and horses; two stars; the constellation Gemini

cultCenter.name: Temple of Castor and Pollux, Roman Forum (Greek cult at Sparta)

family.relation: father (of Pollux; of both in some versions)
family.name: Zeus

plain: Castor and Pollux, the 'Dioscuri', were twin gods who protected sailors. Luke notes that the ship that carried Paul from Malta to Italy had their figure as its emblem. It is a small detail, but a telling one: the prisoner who had just survived shipwreck by trusting God sails on under the badge of the sailors' pagan saviours.
myth: Leda, queen of Sparta, bore twins: Castor, son of her mortal husband Tyndareus, and Pollux (Polydeukes), son of Zeus. When Castor was killed, Pollux begged to share his immortality with his brother, so the two alternated between the underworld and Olympus — or, in another version, became the constellation Gemini. Sailors believed the twins appeared in storms as the electrical glow on masts later called St Elmo's fire, a sign of rescue.
biblicalRole: After three months on Malta, Paul and his companions sailed on 'a ship of Alexandria, which had wintered in the isle, whose sign was Castor and Pollux' (Acts 28:11). Grain ships from Alexandria often carried a carved or painted emblem at the bow. Luke's detail reflects eyewitness precision (the passage is one of the 'we' sections), and readers have often noted the irony: the true protector at sea in the previous chapter was the God whose angel promised Paul safety (Acts 27:23-25).

encounters.title: A ship with the sign of the Twin Brothers
encounters.summary: Paul sails from Malta to Syracuse, Rhegium and Puteoli on an Alexandrian ship whose figurehead was the Dioscuri.

encounters.title: The real protector in the storm
encounters.summary: During the storm, Paul tells the crew that an angel of 'the God to whom I belong' promised that no life would be lost. Everyone reaches land safely.

archaeology.year: excavated in the 19th-20th centuries; three columns have stood since antiquity
archaeology.summary: Founded in 484 BC to thank the twins for victory at Lake Regillus and rebuilt under Tiberius (AD 6). Paul would have walked near it in Rome.

archaeology.find: Dedications by sailors to the Dioscuri
archaeology.place: Greek and Roman ports and islands
archaeology.summary: Votive inscriptions and reliefs thank the twins for safe voyages, confirming their role as patrons of seafarers.

laterFate: The twins' cult faded with paganism, but their stars remain in the Gemini constellation, and St Elmo's fire, once their sign, was transferred to a Christian patron saint of sailors.

name: The Unknown God
original: Greek Agnōstō Theō ('to an unknown god')
domains: an altar to any god not otherwise honoured — insurance against offending an unnamed deity
symbol: An altar inscribed 'To an unknown god'

cultCenter.name: Athens (Paul spoke at the Areopagus)

plain: When Paul visited Athens he noticed an altar inscribed 'To an unknown god'. He used it as the starting point for his speech to the city's council: 'What you worship as unknown, this I proclaim to you.' Ancient writers confirm that Athens had altars to 'unknown gods', though no altar with Paul's exact wording has been found.
myth: There was no myth: the unknown god was not a specific deity. Greeks feared offending gods they did not know about. A story told by Diogenes Laertius (*Lives of the Philosophers* 1.110) says that during a plague the seer Epimenides of Crete let sheep wander from the Areopagus and sacrificed wherever they lay down 'to the appropriate god', so that anonymous altars could still be found around Athens. The travel writer Pausanias (*Description of Greece* 1.1.4) mentions altars 'of the gods called unknown' at the Athenian harbour of Phalerum.
biblicalRole:
In Athens, Paul is 'provoked' by the many idols (Acts 17:16). Invited to explain his teaching at the Areopagus, he says he saw an altar 'To an unknown god' and announces the God whom they worship in ignorance (Acts 17:22-23). He then explains, without quoting Hebrew Scripture, that this God made the world, does not live in temples, needs nothing, made all nations from one man and set their times and boundaries 'so that they should seek God' (Acts 17:24-27). He quotes Greek poets: 'In him we live and move and have our being' (often attributed to Epimenides) and 'For we are also his offspring' (Aratus, *Phaenomena* 5) (Acts 17:28). He ends with a call to repentance and the resurrection, at which some mock, some want to hear more, and a few believe, including Dionysius the Areopagite and a woman named Damaris (Acts 17:30-34).

Ancient sources speak of altars to 'unknown gods' in the plural. Jerome (commentary on Titus 1:12) claimed the inscription actually read 'to the gods of Asia, Europe and Africa, to unknown and foreign gods' and that Paul adapted it to the singular. Others think a single altar with a singular inscription is perfectly plausible. Debated.

encounters.title: Paul's speech at the Areopagus
encounters.summary: Paul uses a pagan altar, Greek poets and the shared human search for God to introduce the Creator and the risen Jesus.

encounters.title: God has overlooked the times of ignorance
encounters.summary: Paul treats paganism as ignorance that God has been patient with, now ended by a call to repent. Romans adds a sterner note: what can be known of God has been suppressed.

archaeology.find: Altar from the sanctuary of Demeter, Pergamum
archaeology.summary: A damaged altar inscription has been restored as 'to the unknown gods' (plural). The restoration depends on filling in missing letters, so it is suggestive rather than certain.

archaeology.year: visible site; bronze plaque of Acts 17 installed in the 20th century
archaeology.summary: Whether Paul spoke on the hill itself or before the council called the Areopagus, which by then often met in the Royal Stoa in the agora, is debated.

laterFate: The unknown god became a famous model for Christian engagement with other cultures: start from what people already sense about God. Dionysius the Areopagite, converted in Acts 17:34, later had influential mystical writings (c. AD 500) falsely attributed to him.

name: Python spirit
original: Greek pythōn, from Pytho, the old name of Delphi
symbol: The serpent Python coiled around the omphalos stone at Delphi; Apollo's tripod

cultCenter.name: Delphi (Pytho), oracle of Apollo

plain: In Philippi, Paul met a slave girl who had a 'spirit of python' and earned her owners money by fortune-telling. The name comes from the great serpent Python, killed by Apollo at Delphi, home of the most famous oracle in the Greek world. Paul commanded the spirit to leave her in Jesus' name, and her owners had Paul and Silas beaten and jailed.
myth: According to Greek myth, the serpent (or dragon) Python guarded the ancient oracle at Pytho, later called Delphi. The young god Apollo killed it with his arrows and took over the oracle, which was then delivered through his priestess, the Pythia. The Pythian Games commemorated the victory. By the Roman era, 'python' had also become a popular word for someone who spoke oracles from inside themselves; Plutarch (*On the Obsolescence of Oracles* 9) notes that ventriloquists were then called 'pythons'.
biblicalRole:
Luke writes that the girl had *pneuma pythōna*, literally 'a spirit, a python' (Acts 16:16). Older translations soften this to 'a spirit of divination'. For several days she followed Paul's group crying, 'These men are servants of the Most High God, who show us the way of salvation' (Acts 16:17). Her words were true, but Paul, 'greatly annoyed', commanded the spirit in the name of Jesus Christ to come out, and it left 'that very hour' (Acts 16:18). Her owners, seeing their profit gone, dragged Paul and Silas to the magistrates, who had them beaten and imprisoned (Acts 16:19-24) — leading to the earthquake and the jailer's conversion.

Luke presents the spirit as a real power, not a trick, while treating its source as unclean. The Old Testament had already forbidden divination and consulting mediums (Deut 18:10-12); the Greek translation uses *engastrimythos* ('belly-talker') for the medium at Endor (1 Sam 28:7), the same kind of figure later called a 'python'.

encounters.title: The slave girl of Philippi
encounters.summary: A fortune-telling girl proclaims Paul's mission; Paul casts out the python spirit in Jesus' name.

encounters.title: Profits lost, apostles jailed
encounters.summary: Her owners turn a spiritual event into a legal charge. In prison, Paul and Silas sing, an earthquake opens the doors, and the jailer believes.

encounters.title: Divination forbidden
encounters.summary: The Law and Prophets reject seeking hidden knowledge through mediums and spirits rather than from God.

archaeology.find: Sanctuary of Apollo at Delphi ('Great Excavation')
archaeology.summary: The French moved a whole village to uncover the temple of Apollo, treasuries, theatre and stadium. A stone omphalos ('navel of the world') was also found.
A bronze column of three intertwined serpents, dedicated at Delphi after the Greek victory at Plataea in 479 BC and moved by Constantine to his new capital.
A letter of the emperor Claudius naming Gallio as proconsul of Achaia, found at Delphi. It is the key anchor for dating Paul's time in Corinth (Acts 18:12), about a year after his visit to Philippi.

renamed.biblical: 'a spirit of divination' (KJV and most translations)
renamed.explanation: Translators usually explain the term rather than transliterate it, which hides the link with Delphi and Apollo.

laterFate: The Delphic oracle declined in the Roman era and was closed under Christian emperors around AD 390. In modern charismatic teaching 'python spirit' is sometimes used for a supposed spirit that 'squeezes' spiritual life; this is a modern devotional idea, not what the word meant in Acts.

name: The golden calf
otherNames: the calves of Bethel and Dan
original: Hebrew ʿegel massekah ('molten calf'); ʿegel means a young bull
domains: image of the God who brought Israel out of Egypt (or his throne)
royal state religion of the northern kingdom
symbol: A young bull cast in metal or wood overlaid with gold

cultCenter.name: Bethel (royal sanctuary of the northern kingdom); also Dan

plain: The golden calf was a bull image made twice in Israel's story: once by Aaron at Mount Sinai, and again centuries later by King Jeroboam, who set up two calves at Bethel and Dan. Both times the people were told, 'Here are your gods, O Israel, who brought you up out of Egypt.' The striking thing is that the calf was not presented as a foreign god but as a way of worshipping Israel's own God — which is exactly what the Bible condemns.
myth: There is no myth of the calf itself. In the ancient Near East the young bull was a common symbol of strength and fertility and was linked with gods such as El ('Bull El' at Ugarit) and the storm god Baal-Hadad, who was often shown standing on a bull. Gods were frequently pictured riding or standing on animals, so a bull could be an image of a god or a pedestal for an invisible one.
biblicalRole:
**At Sinai.** While Moses is on the mountain, the people ask Aaron to 'make us gods (elohim) who shall go before us'. He melts their gold earrings and makes a calf; they say, 'These are your gods, O Israel, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt.' Aaron builds an altar and announces, 'Tomorrow is a feast to the LORD (Yahweh)' (Exod 32:1-6). Moses breaks the tablets, burns and grinds the calf, scatters it on water and makes the people drink it (Exod 32:19-20). The Levites kill about three thousand (Exod 32:28). Israel later remembers this as its defining apostasy: 'they exchanged their glory for the image of an ox that eats grass' (Ps 106:19-20; Deut 9:16; Neh 9:18; Acts 7:41).

**Jeroboam's calves.** When the kingdom split (c. 930 BC), Jeroboam feared his people would return to Jerusalem's temple. He made two golden calves, put one in Bethel and one in Dan, and used the same words: 'Behold your gods, O Israel, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt' (1 Kgs 12:28-30). He appointed non-Levite priests and a new festival (1 Kgs 12:31-33). From then on, 'the sin of Jeroboam' is the standard by which Kings judges every northern king (for example 2 Kgs 10:29; 2 Kgs 17:21-22). Hosea mocks: 'Men who sacrifice kiss calves!' (Hos 13:2; Hos 8:5-6).

**What were the calves?** Three main views:
1. **Pedestal view** (W. F. Albright and many since): the calves were thrones or mounts for the invisible Yahweh, like the cherubim of the ark. The sin was making an image that blurred into idolatry.
2. **Image of Yahweh**: the calf represented Yahweh himself in bull form, against the command not to make images of God (Exod 20:4).
3. **Foreign influence**: the calf copied the Egyptian Apis or Hathor (Sinai) or the Canaanite El/Baal bull (Bethel). Jeroboam had spent time in Egypt (1 Kgs 11:40).
Many scholars combine 1 and 3. Many also suspect that the Sinai story was written or shaped with Jeroboam's calves in view, because of the identical slogan; traditional readers take the Sinai event as historical and Jeroboam as deliberately reviving it. Debated.

encounters.title: Aaron's calf at Sinai
encounters.summary: A 'feast to the LORD' around a golden calf breaks the covenant just made. Moses intercedes and the people are spared destruction, but judgement falls.

encounters.title: Moses recalls the calf
encounters.summary: Moses tells the next generation how he ground the calf to dust and threw it into the brook, and how he prayed forty days for Aaron and the people.

encounters.title: Jeroboam sets up calves at Bethel and Dan
encounters.summary: A political move to keep the northern tribes away from Jerusalem becomes the northern kingdom's founding sin. Chronicles says Levites fled south as a result.

encounters.title: A prophet at Bethel's altar
encounters.summary: A man of God predicts that a king named Josiah will burn bones on Bethel's altar; three centuries later Josiah does so.

encounters.title: Prophets against the calves
encounters.summary: Hosea predicts the calf of Samaria will be carried to Assyria as tribute; Amos preaches at Bethel, 'the king's sanctuary', and is told to go home.

encounters.title: Remembered in the New Testament
encounters.summary: Stephen calls the calf a turning back to Egypt in the heart; Paul quotes Exod 32:6 as a warning to Christians tempted by idol feasts.

archaeology.summary: A small bronze calf partly plated with silver, found with its pottery shrine, from about 1600 BC (Canaanite period). It shows how calf images were used in Canaanite religion centuries before Israel's kings.
A bronze bull figurine (about 18 cm long) at an open-air cult site from about 1200 BC, in the region of the early Israelite settlements. Whether the worshippers were Israelites is debated.

archaeology.find: Cultic platform (high place) at Tel Dan
archaeology.summary: A large stone platform, horned altar and sacred enclosure, rebuilt in several phases from the 10th-9th century BC onward, widely identified with the royal sanctuary of Dan where Jeroboam placed a calf. No calf was found.

laterFate: Assyria conquered the north in 722 BC; Hosea had predicted that the calf would be carried away (Hos 10:5-6). Josiah defiled the altar at Bethel about a century later (2 Kgs 23:15). In Jewish tradition the calf became the archetypal sin, said to leave a trace in every later punishment; Christian writers used it as a picture of any attempt to worship God on one's own terms.

name: Nehushtan
original: Hebrew Neḥushtan — a play on neḥoshet ('bronze') and naḥash ('serpent')
domains: a sign of God's saving power (in Num 21)
later, an object of incense offerings
symbol: A bronze (copper alloy) snake mounted on a pole

cultCenter.name: Temple in Jerusalem, until Hezekiah's reform

plain: Nehushtan was the bronze serpent Moses made in the wilderness so that people bitten by snakes could look at it and live. Israel kept it for about five hundred years, until people were burning incense to it. King Hezekiah smashed it and called it Nehushtan — roughly 'that bronze thing'. Jesus later compared his own lifting up on the cross to the serpent on the pole.
myth: Nehushtan has no myth outside the Bible. Snake imagery was widespread and ambiguous in the ancient Near East: serpents could be deadly enemies (like the Egyptian chaos-serpent Apophis) or protective and healing (like the Egyptian uraeus cobra, or later the snake of the Greek healing god Asclepius). Winged serpents called seraphim appear on Judahite seals of the 8th century BC.
biblicalRole:
**In the wilderness.** When Israel complains against God and Moses, 'fiery serpents' (seraphim) bite the people and many die. When they confess, God tells Moses to make a fiery serpent and set it on a pole; anyone bitten who looks at it lives. Moses makes a serpent of bronze (Num 21:4-9). The healing comes from God's promise, not the metal.

**In the temple.** Centuries later, Hezekiah 'broke in pieces the bronze serpent that Moses had made, for unto those days the children of Israel did burn incense to it; and he called it Nehushtan' (2 Kgs 18:4). An object once used by God became an idol because people treated it as a source of power in itself.

**In the New Testament.** Jesus tells Nicodemus, 'As Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, even so must the Son of Man be lifted up, that whoever believes in him may have eternal life' (John 3:14-15). Paul uses the serpent episode as a warning against testing Christ (1 Cor 10:9).

**Scholarly questions.** Some historians think the temple serpent was originally a Canaanite or Egyptian-style healing emblem, and that the Num 21 story explained its presence; others accept the story as the true origin. Whether Hezekiah coined the name or it was already in use is also debated.

encounters.title: Look and live
encounters.summary: In the wilderness, God provides healing through a bronze serpent on a pole. The cure requires only looking in trust.

encounters.title: Hezekiah smashes Nehushtan
encounters.summary: Among Hezekiah's reforms: high places removed, pillars broken, the Asherah cut down, and Moses' serpent destroyed because it had become an object of worship.

encounters.title: The Son of Man lifted up
encounters.summary: Jesus uses the serpent on the pole as a picture of his crucifixion: the sign of the curse becomes the means of healing for those who believe.

encounters.title: Do not test the Lord
encounters.summary: Paul warns the Corinthians by recalling those destroyed by serpents.

archaeology.find: Copper snake from the Timna shrine
archaeology.summary: In an Egyptian Hathor mining shrine later converted (probably by Midianites) into a tent shrine, excavators found a copper snake about 12 cm long with a gilded head, from about the 12th century BC. Many scholars note the parallel with Moses' bronze serpent and with his Midianite in-laws (Exod 3:1), though a direct link cannot be proven.

Seals of the 8th century BC show four-winged and two-winged cobras (uraei), probably the 'seraphim' imagery behind Isa 6:2, Isa 14:29 and Isa 30:6. They show serpent imagery in royal Judah in Hezekiah's era.
A small bronze snake from a Late Bronze Age context, one of several serpent objects found in Canaanite cities.

renamed.explanation: The name combines the words for bronze and serpent. Many readers take Hezekiah's naming as dismissive — 'a mere piece of bronze' — though the Hebrew could also mean that this was already its name. Debated.

laterFate: The serpent on a pole became a Christian symbol of the cross. The Greek healing staff of Asclepius (one snake on a rod) is sometimes linked with it in popular writing, but the two traditions developed separately. Several churches have claimed to own Moses' serpent, including the Basilica of Sant'Ambrogio in Milan, whose bronze snake is actually Byzantine.

name: Teraphim
original: Hebrew terafim (a plural form, even for one object); etymology uncertain
domains: possibly ancestor veneration and family inheritance
symbol: A figurine, small enough to hide in a saddle bag or, in one case, large enough to look like a person in bed

cultCenter.name: Household shrines (no central sanctuary); shown at Haran, Gen 31

plain: Teraphim were household god-images kept in family homes, used for protection and for asking guidance. Rachel stole her father Laban's teraphim; Michal used one to fool Saul's soldiers; and the prophets condemned teraphim as useless. They show that ordinary family religion in Israel often mixed devotion to Yahweh with other practices.
myth: There is no myth. The meaning of the word is debated: suggestions include a link to the Rephaim (the dead ancestors), to a Hittite word *tarpi* (a spirit), or to a root meaning 'decay', used mockingly ('rotten things'). Many scholars today think teraphim were images of deceased ancestors consulted for guidance, but this is not certain.
biblicalRole:
**Rachel and Laban.** As Jacob's family secretly leaves Haran, Rachel steals her father's teraphim. Laban pursues them, calling them 'my gods'. Rachel hides them in a camel saddle, sits on them and says she cannot get up because 'the way of women' is upon her (Gen 31:19; Gen 31:30-35). The scene ridicules the 'gods' — they are sat on by a supposedly unclean woman. Later Jacob tells his household to put away foreign gods, and buries them at Shechem (Gen 35:2-4).

**Michal and David.** Michal lets David escape through a window and puts the teraphim in his bed with goat hair at its head to deceive Saul's messengers (1 Sam 19:11-16). That a teraphim was in David's house at all is striking.

**Micah and the Danites.** In Judges, Micah of Ephraim makes an ephod and teraphim for his private shrine; the tribe of Dan steals them and his priest for their new city (Judg 17:5; Judg 18:14-20).

**Condemnation and divination.** Samuel equates stubbornness with 'iniquity and teraphim' (1 Sam 15:23). Josiah removes them in his reform (2 Kgs 23:24). Ezekiel says the king of Babylon 'consulted the teraphim' at a crossroads (Ezek 21:21), and Zechariah says 'the teraphim have spoken vanity' (Zech 10:2). Hosea lists teraphim with ephod and pillar among things Israel will be without during exile (Hos 3:4), a puzzling verse that some read as neutral.

**Why did Rachel steal them?** Older scholarship (from Cyrus Gordon in the 1930s) cited the Nuzi tablets to argue that holding the household gods gave a claim to the family inheritance. Later studies (Moshe Greenberg, 1962, and others) weakened this reading. Other suggestions: for protection on the journey, to stop Laban divining where they went, or simple devotion. Debated.

encounters.title: Rachel steals Laban's gods
encounters.summary: Laban searches the tents for his household gods; Rachel sits on them. The story mocks gods that cannot protect themselves.

encounters.title: Foreign gods buried at Shechem
encounters.summary: Before going to Bethel, Jacob tells his household to put away their foreign gods and buries them under the oak by Shechem.

encounters.title: Michal's decoy in David's bed
encounters.summary: A teraphim with goats' hair stands in for David, buying him time to escape.

encounters.title: Micah's shrine and the Danites
encounters.summary: A household shrine with ephod and teraphim becomes the cult of a whole tribe in a period when 'every man did what was right in his own eyes'.

encounters.title: Teraphim condemned and removed
encounters.summary: Prophets and reformers treat teraphim as idolatry and as a source of false guidance.

archaeology.summary: Family adoption and inheritance contracts mention household gods (ilanu) passing to the principal heir. Once taken as the key to Rachel's theft, this link is now considered weaker.

archaeology.find: Emar texts on 'the gods and the dead'
archaeology.summary: Wills from the late Bronze Age require the heir to honour 'the gods and the dead' of the family, supporting the view that household gods were connected with ancestor veneration.

archaeology.year: excavated by the thousand since the early 20th century
archaeology.summary: Small clay female figurines from 8th-7th century BC homes show household religion was common. They are usually linked with Asherah or with fertility and protection rather than identified as teraphim.

laterFate: Teraphim disappear from Jewish religious practice after the exile. Rabbinic commentators puzzled over them; one later legend claimed they were mummified human heads that spoke, a medieval invention.

name: Gad and Meni
original: Hebrew Gad ('fortune, luck') and Meni ('allotment, destiny', from manah, 'to count/assign')
symbol: A table spread with food and mixed wine set out for the gods

cultCenter.name: Popular across Syria and Arabia; best attested at Palmyra (the Gad cult)

plain: Gad and Meni were gods of Luck and Destiny. In Isaiah, God condemns those who 'set a table for Fortune and fill cups of mixed wine for Destiny'. The prophet then turns the word for destiny into a pun: 'I will destine you to the sword.'
myth: There are no myths. 'Gad' was a common Semitic word for good fortune, and the god Gad was a personified luck-spirit, often the protecting fortune of a person or city, similar to the Greek Tyche. Meni is less well known; some scholars connect it with Manat, a pre-Islamic Arabian goddess of fate, but the link is uncertain.
biblicalRole:
Isaiah addresses those 'who forsake the LORD, who forget my holy mountain, who set a table for Gad and fill cups of mixed wine for Meni' (Isa 65:11). The next verse plays on the second name: 'I will destine (maniti) you to the sword' (Isa 65:12). The point: if you trust in Destiny, God will give you a destiny — just not the one you hoped for. The KJV translated the names as common nouns, 'that troop' and 'that number', which hides the gods. Modern translations print Fortune and Destiny or Gad and Meni.

The word gad also appears in names. When Leah's maid bore a son, Leah said 'Good fortune comes!' and named him Gad (Gen 30:11). Places such as Baal-gad (Josh 11:17) and Migdal-gad (Josh 15:37) show the word in religious and place names. Whether these refer to the deity or just to 'luck' is debated.

encounters.title: A table for Fortune
encounters.summary: Isaiah condemns a meal offered to luck-gods by people who have forgotten Yahweh, and turns Destiny's name into a sentence of judgement.

encounters.title: Gad, son of Jacob
encounters.summary: Leah names Zilpah's son Gad, 'fortune'. Jacob's blessing later puns on the same name with another root: 'Gad, a troop (gedud) shall raid him'.

encounters.title: Gad in place names
encounters.summary: Baal-gad near Mount Hermon and Migdal-gad in Judah may preserve the worship of a fortune-god, or simply the word 'luck'.

archaeology.summary: Administrative notes of the 8th century BC include the personal name Gaddiyau ('Yahweh is my fortune'), showing gad as a name element in Israel.

archaeology.find: Relief of the Gad of Dura
archaeology.summary: A relief dedicated in AD 159 shows the Gad (fortune) of the city enthroned, crowned by its founder — evidence of how widespread fortune-gods were in the Semitic world.

archaeology.place: Hegra (Mada'in Salih), Arabia, and Nabataean sites
archaeology.summary: Nabataean tomb inscriptions invoke Manawat, a fate goddess; some scholars connect her with Meni. The connection is speculative.

renamed.explanation: The King James translators read the words as ordinary nouns. Modern scholarship recognises them as divine names, partly because of the pun in Isa 65:12.

laterFate: Gad remained a popular luck-spirit in Syria into the Roman period. In later Hebrew and Aramaic, gad still meant 'fortune', and the Talmud mentions popular customs honouring 'luck' that the rabbis treated as superstition. Belief in luck and fate as personal powers continues in many cultures.

name: Azazel
original: Hebrew ʿazaʾzel; meaning debated
domains: the removal of Israel's sins on the Day of Atonement
in later Jewish writings, a fallen angel who taught forbidden arts
symbol: A goat driven into the desert

cultCenter.name: The Judean wilderness east of Jerusalem (no cult; destination of the goat)

plain: On the Day of Atonement, Israel's high priest cast lots over two goats: one 'for the LORD', sacrificed as a sin offering, and one 'for Azazel', sent alive into the wilderness carrying the people's sins. Nobody is sure what Azazel means. It may be the name of a desert demon, the name of a place, or a word meaning 'complete removal'.
myth: The Bible tells no story about Azazel. Later Jewish writings do. In *1 Enoch* (3rd-2nd century BC), Asael (Azazel in later copies) is one of the rebel angels, the Watchers, who taught humans to make weapons, jewellery and cosmetics; God orders the angel Raphael to bind him hand and foot and throw him into darkness in the desert under jagged rocks until the judgement (1 Enoch 8:1; 10:4-8). This links the Day of Atonement goat with the angels of Gen 6. In the *Apocalypse of Abraham* (1st-2nd century AD), Azazel is an unclean bird and the tempter. A Qumran text (4Q180) also refers to Azazel and the angels.
biblicalRole:
Leviticus 16 describes the Day of Atonement. Aaron takes two goats and casts lots: 'one lot for the LORD, and the other lot for Azazel' (Lev 16:8). The LORD's goat is killed as a sin offering. Aaron lays both hands on the head of the live goat, confesses over it 'all the iniquities of the children of Israel', and a man sends it away into the wilderness, 'to a land not inhabited' (Lev 16:20-22). The man who released it must wash before returning to camp (Lev 16:26).

Three main readings of 'Azazel':
1. **A desert demon.** The parallel 'for the LORD / for Azazel' suggests a personal being. On this view the goat does not worship Azazel but returns sin to the realm of chaos and evil, its proper home. The very next chapter forbids sacrificing to goat-demons (seʿirim, Lev 17:7), which shows how carefully the rite was framed.
2. **A place name**, a rugged cliff or 'precipice'. Rabbinic tradition (Mishnah *Yoma* 6:6) says the goat was later pushed over a cliff.
3. **An abstract noun**, 'for complete removal'. The Greek translation and the Latin Vulgate render it with ideas of 'sending away', which led to the English 'scapegoat' (William Tyndale's coinage, 'escape goat').
All three have serious defenders. Debated.

**Christian reading.** Hebrews compares Jesus' sacrifice with the Day of Atonement (Heb 9:7; Heb 9:11-12) and notes that sin-offering bodies were burned 'outside the camp', as Jesus suffered outside the gate (Heb 13:11-12). Many Christian writers saw the scapegoat as a picture of Christ carrying sins away (Isa 53:6), while some Seventh-day Adventist teaching has identified the Azazel goat with Satan, who bears final responsibility for sin — a reading most other traditions reject.

encounters.title: Two goats and a lot
encounters.summary: One goat dies for the LORD; the other carries Israel's confessed sins into the wilderness 'for Azazel'.

encounters.title: No more sacrifices to goat-demons
encounters.summary: Israel must stop offering sacrifices to the seʿirim; Jeroboam later appoints priests for them. Azazel's goat must not be confused with such offerings.

encounters.title: Sin carried away
encounters.summary: The idea of sin being removed far away is echoed in the Psalms and reapplied in the New Testament to Jesus.

archaeology.year: 1952 (Qumran Cave 4); published by J. T. Milik, 1976
archaeology.summary: Aramaic copies of the Book of the Watchers, from as early as the 3rd-2nd century BC, contain the leader Asael and his punishment in the desert, showing how early the angel-reading of Azazel developed.
A Dead Sea Scrolls text mentions 'Azazel and the angels' who loved the daughters of men, linking Lev 16 and Gen 6.

renamed.explanation: Following the Latin caper emissarius, Tyndale coined 'scapegoat' (the goat that escapes), and the KJV followed. Most modern translations keep 'Azazel', leaving the meaning open.

laterFate: In Jewish tradition the goat ritual ended with the destruction of the temple in AD 70; Yom Kippur continues with prayer and fasting. The word 'scapegoat' entered English with the general meaning of someone blamed for others, and the French thinker René Girard built a theory of culture and violence around it. Milton made Azazel a standard-bearer of Satan's army.

name: Lilith
original: Hebrew lilit; compare Akkadian lilītu, a female wind-demon
domains: in later Jewish folklore, a danger to newborns and to men sleeping alone
symbol: In Isaiah, a creature of ruined places; in later amulets, a bound female demon

cultCenter.name: No cult; Isa 34 sets her in the ruins of Edom (shown at Bozrah)

plain: The word lilit appears only once in the Bible, in Isaiah's picture of ruined Edom, where wild animals live and 'the lilit' finds a resting place. Older translations call it a screech owl; many modern ones say Lilith or 'night creature'. The famous legend that Lilith was Adam's first wife comes from a medieval Jewish text, not from the Bible.
myth: In Mesopotamia, lilû and lilītu were wind or storm spirits (from *lil*, 'wind'), later imagined as demons who preyed on women and infants. Aramaic incantation bowls from Babylonia (5th-7th centuries AD) ask for protection against 'liliths', sometimes issuing them a bill of divorce. The story that Lilith was Adam's first wife, created from the earth like him, who refused to lie beneath him and fled, comes from the *Alphabet of Ben Sira*, a satirical Hebrew work of about the 8th-10th century AD. It was then developed in Kabbalah and, in the twentieth century, reclaimed by some feminist writers as a symbol of independence.
biblicalRole:
Isaiah 34 is an oracle of judgement on Edom: the land becomes a wilderness of thorns where jackals, ostriches and wild goats live. 'There also shall the lilit rest, and find for herself a place of rest' (Isa 34:14). In the poetic list, the lilit is one of the creatures that inhabit a land God has left desolate.

Translations differ: 'screech owl' (KJV), 'night monster' (ASV), 'night creature' (NIV), 'Lilith' (NRSV), 'night bird' (ESV). The choice depends on whether the list is entirely of animals, or of animals and demons together. Since the same verse mentions seʿirim, which can mean wild goats or goat-demons (compare Isa 13:21), many scholars think Isaiah is mixing real animals with demonic figures that people believed haunted ruins. Others read every item as an animal. Debated.

Nothing in Genesis mentions Lilith. Some later readers explained the two creation accounts (Gen 1:27 and Gen 2:21-22) by imagining a first wife; this is a later interpretation, not the text's meaning.

encounters.title: A resting place in ruined Edom
encounters.summary: Isaiah's poem of desolation lists wild creatures that take over the ruins of Edom, including the lilit.

encounters.title: Creatures of the ruins
encounters.summary: A similar oracle against Babylon pictures ostriches, wild goats (or goat-demons) and howling creatures in its ruins.

archaeology.year: 1888-1900 (Nippur excavations); published by J. A. Montgomery, 1913
archaeology.summary: Clay bowls buried under house floors, inscribed in spirals with spells against liliths and other demons, often written for Jewish clients.
Hymns meant to frighten away evil spirits list 'liliths' among them, showing the term was understood as a demon by the 1st century BC.

Small limestone plaques of about the 7th century BC with Phoenician spells against flying demons that attack at night. Some scholars have questioned their authenticity; their link to Lilith is indirect.

archaeology.year: known since the 1930s; British Museum since 2003
archaeology.summary: A winged goddess with owls and lions, about 1800 BC. Popular books call her Lilith, but most specialists identify her as Ishtar or Ereshkigal.

renamed.explanation: Translators disagree over whether the word names a bird or a demon. The KJV's bird is one guess among several.

laterFate: Lilith became a major figure of Jewish folklore: amulets protected mothers and babies by naming three angels said to have chased her. In modern culture she appears in literature, art and music, often as a symbol of female independence, a meaning far from both Isaiah and medieval legend.

name: Shedim
original: Hebrew shedim (plural of shed); from Akkadian šēdu
symbol: In Mesopotamia, the šēdu appears as a winged, human-headed bull or lion guarding gateways

cultCenter.name: Mesopotamian palace gateways guarded by šēdu/lamassu (shown at Khorsabad)

plain: Shedim is a Hebrew word for spirit-powers that the Bible uses twice, both times for the beings that Israel actually sacrificed to when it worshipped other gods. It comes from the Mesopotamian word for a protective spirit — the kind shown as giant winged bulls at palace gates. The Greek translators rendered it 'demons', and Paul uses the same idea: idols are nothing, but what is sacrificed to them is offered to demons.
myth: In Mesopotamia a šēdu was a protective, usually good spirit, often paired with a lamassu. Huge stone guardians with bulls' or lions' bodies, wings and human heads stood at the gates of Assyrian palaces to ward off evil. A person's šēdu could also be a personal spirit of vitality. The Hebrew Bible borrows the word but gives it a negative meaning: these are not protectors but false objects of worship.
biblicalRole:
**Deuteronomy 32.** In the Song of Moses: 'They sacrificed to shedim, not to God (eloah), to gods (elohim) they had not known, to new gods that came newly up' (Deut 32:17). The verse affirms that there was something real receiving these sacrifices, while denying that they were God.

**Psalm 106.** Recalling Israel's sins in the land: 'They sacrificed their sons and their daughters to the shedim, and shed innocent blood… whom they sacrificed to the idols of Canaan' (Ps 106:37-38). Here the shedim are linked to child sacrifice.

**From gods to demons.** The Greek Septuagint translated shedim as *daimonia* and even rendered Ps 96:5, 'all the gods of the nations are idols (elilim)', as 'all the gods of the nations are demons'. Paul draws directly on Deut 32:17: 'What the pagans sacrifice they sacrifice to demons and not to God' (1 Cor 10:20), even though 'an idol is nothing in the world' (1 Cor 8:4). Revelation likewise condemns the worship of 'demons and idols of gold' (Rev 9:20).

**How to understand it.** Some scholars, including those who emphasise the divine-council reading, see the shedim as real lesser spiritual beings standing behind the nations' gods (compare Deut 32:8 in the Dead Sea Scrolls). Others read the language as Israel's way of saying that foreign gods are spiritually dangerous without granting them true divinity. Both readings take Paul's 'idols are nothing / demons are real' tension seriously. Debated.

encounters.title: Sacrificing to non-gods
encounters.summary: Moses' song predicts that Israel will grow fat and forsake the Rock, offering sacrifices to shedim.

encounters.title: Sons and daughters sacrificed to the shedim
encounters.summary: The psalm connects worship of Canaan's idols with child sacrifice and calls the recipients shedim.

encounters.title: Not partners with demons
encounters.summary: Paul affirms that there is one God and that idols are nothing, yet warns that idol feasts are fellowship with demons.

encounters.title: Worshipping demons
encounters.summary: Revelation and the Law both describe idolatry as service to evil spiritual powers.

archaeology.year: 1843-1844 (Paul-Émile Botta, Khorsabad); 1845-1851 (Austen Henry Layard, Nimrud and Nineveh)
archaeology.summary: Colossal human-headed winged bulls guarded Assyrian palace gates in the age of Israel's kings. They are now in the Louvre, the British Museum and elsewhere, and show what the Akkadian word behind 'shedim' first meant.
Spells written for Jewish, Christian and Mandaean clients name shedim among the demons to be bound, showing the later, fully demonic meaning.

laterFate: In rabbinic literature shedim became a broad class of demons, said in one tradition to have been created at twilight on the sixth day of creation (Mishnah *Avot* 5:6 lists things created at that hour, and later sources include demons). The word continues in Jewish folklore and modern Hebrew.

name: The sons of God
original: Hebrew bene (ha-)elohim / bene elim / bene elyon
domains: in some readings, rulers over the nations
symbol: A heavenly assembly around God's throne; the stars ('morning stars', Job 38:7)

cultCenter.name: Mount Hermon, where 1 Enoch sets the Watchers' descent

plain: Several Old Testament passages speak of 'the sons of God' — heavenly beings who gather before God's throne. They shout for joy at creation, present themselves before God with 'the satan' in Job, and are judged in Psalm 82. In Genesis 6 'sons of God' take human wives, and readers have argued for two thousand years over whether they were angels, the godly line of Seth, or human kings.
myth: At Ugarit (13th century BC) the gods were called 'the sons of El' and met in 'the assembly of El', with El as their aged father-king. Mesopotamian myths also describe divine assemblies. The biblical sons of God share the vocabulary but are subordinate to one God who created them, not his offspring by birth.
biblicalRole:
**Heavenly court passages.**
- Job 1:6 and Job 2:1: 'the sons of God came to present themselves before the LORD', and 'the satan' came among them.
- Job 38:7: at creation 'the morning stars sang together, and all the sons of God shouted for joy'.
- Ps 29:1 and Ps 89:6-7: the 'sons of the mighty' (bene elim) are called to praise, and God is feared in 'the council of the holy ones'.
- Ps 82: 'God stands in the divine assembly; he judges among the gods (elohim)… I said, You are gods, all of you sons of the Most High; nevertheless you shall die like men' (Ps 82:1; Ps 82:6-7).
- Deut 32:8: in the Masoretic Hebrew, God divided the nations 'according to the number of the sons of Israel'; a Dead Sea Scroll (4QDeut-j) reads 'sons of God', and the Septuagint has 'angels/sons of God'. Many modern translations (ESV, NRSV) follow 'sons of God'.

**Genesis 6:1-4.** 'The sons of God saw the daughters of men… and took them wives', and the Nephilim were on the earth. Three main readings:
1. **Angelic view**: rebellious heavenly beings married human women. This was the dominant Jewish view in the Second Temple period (1 Enoch 6-16, Jubilees) and among early Christian writers such as Justin Martyr and Tertullian. Jude 1:6 and 2 Pet 2:4 are often read as alluding to it.
2. **Sethite view**: the godly line of Seth intermarried with the line of Cain. It became dominant in Christianity after Julius Africanus and especially Augustine (*City of God* 15.23).
3. **Royal / human-ruler view**: powerful kings who claimed divine status took harems. Found in some Targums and rabbinic sources (which render 'sons of the great ones'), and among some modern scholars.
All three have serious defenders. Debated.

**Jesus and Psalm 82.** Jesus quotes 'I said, you are gods' (John 10:34-36). How the argument works depends on who the 'gods' are — divine beings, human judges, or Israel at Sinai. Debated.

The 'divine council' framework (associated in popular form with Michael Heiser, and in academic form with scholars such as E. T. Mullen and Mark S. Smith) treats these beings as real elohim set over the nations. Critics argue this risks reading later angelology back into the texts, or prefer to see Ps 82 as addressing human judges, or read the Old Testament's language as moving toward strict monotheism. See the council study for the full debate.

encounters.title: Sons of God and daughters of men
encounters.summary: A brief, puzzling episode before the flood, read as angels, Sethites, or kings.

encounters.title: The heavenly court in Job
encounters.summary: The sons of God attend God's court, where the accuser challenges Job's integrity; they rejoiced when God laid the earth's foundations.

encounters.title: God judges the gods
encounters.summary: God condemns members of his assembly for unjust rule and declares they will die like men; Jesus later cites the psalm in a dispute.

encounters.title: Nations allotted to the sons of God
encounters.summary: In the Qumran and Greek text, the nations are divided by the number of the sons of God, while Israel is the LORD's own portion. Daniel's 'princes' of Persia and Greece are often read in this light.

encounters.title: Watchers and imprisoned angels
encounters.summary: Daniel's 'watchers' and the New Testament's angels kept in chains are linked by many interpreters with Gen 6. How directly Jude and Peter depend on 1 Enoch is debated, though Jude quotes Enoch in Jude 1:14-15.

archaeology.find: Ugaritic tablets describing the assembly of El
archaeology.summary: Texts speak of 'the sons of El' and 'the assembly of the gods', supplying the vocabulary behind the biblical 'sons of God'.
A Hebrew manuscript reads 'sons of God' in Deut 32:8 where the later Masoretic text reads 'sons of Israel', confirming that the Septuagint was translating a real Hebrew reading.
Copies of 1 Enoch 6-16 tell of two hundred Watchers who descended on Mount Hermon, showing the angelic reading of Gen 6 was established by the 3rd-2nd century BC.

laterFate: The idea of a heavenly court continued in Jewish and Christian angelology. Revelation pictures God enthroned among twenty-four elders and living creatures (Rev 4:4-11). In the New Testament, believers are called 'sons of God' through faith (Gal 3:26; Rom 8:14), and Paul says they will judge angels (1 Cor 6:3). Since the late 20th century, the divine council has become a major topic of both academic and popular study.

name: The satan (the accuser)
original: Hebrew ha-śaṭan ('the adversary/accuser'); Greek diabolos ('slanderer')
domains: accusation and testing in God's court (Old Testament)
opposition to God and his people (New Testament)
symbol: In Scripture, an accuser standing at the right hand; later the dragon and ancient serpent (Rev 12:9)

cultCenter.name: No cult; the heavenly court of Zech 3 is set over Jerusalem

plain: In Hebrew, satan is a common word meaning 'adversary' or 'accuser'. In Job and Zechariah, 'the satan' — with the definite article, so a job title rather than a name — is a member of God's court who challenges the righteous. By the New Testament, Satan has become the proper name of the chief enemy of God, the devil. How that development happened is an important question.
myth: The Bible has no single origin story for Satan. Later Jewish and Christian traditions filled the gap: some linked him to the Watchers of Gen 6, others to the serpent of Gen 3, and later Christian interpreters read Isa 14:12-15 (the fall of the 'morning star', the king of Babylon) and Ezek 28:12-19 (the king of Tyre in Eden) as describing Satan's pre-creation fall. Those two prophecies are addressed to human kings in context; reading them as Satan's story is an ancient interpretation, not their plain subject. Debated.
biblicalRole:
**satan as a common noun.** The angel of the LORD stands in Balaam's way 'as a satan (adversary)' (Num 22:22; Num 22:32). Philistine commanders fear David might become 'a satan' to them in battle (1 Sam 29:4). God raises up Hadad the Edomite as 'a satan' to Solomon (1 Kgs 11:14). An accuser stands at a man's right hand (Ps 109:6).

**The satan in God's court.** In Job, 'the satan' comes with the sons of God and asks, 'Does Job fear God for nothing?' He is allowed to test Job within limits God sets (Job 1:6-12; Job 2:1-7). In Zechariah's vision, the satan stands to accuse the high priest Joshua, and the LORD rebukes him (Zech 3:1-2). In both, he is an accuser operating with God's permission, not an independent evil god.

**A shift in Chronicles.** In 2 Sam 24:1 the LORD incites David to take a census; the later retelling says 'Satan (no article) stood up against Israel and provoked David' (1 Chr 21:1). Many scholars see a move toward a personal name and toward attributing evil impulses to an adversary rather than directly to God; others think the word still means 'an adversary' here. Debated.

**New Testament.** Satan tempts Jesus (Matt 4:1-11), is seen 'fall like lightning from heaven' (Luke 10:18), is 'the ruler of this world' who is cast out (John 12:31), and is 'the accuser of our brothers' thrown down (Rev 12:9-10), identified with 'that ancient serpent'. The Pharisees accuse Jesus of casting out demons by Beelzebul, and Jesus answers by speaking of Satan's kingdom (Mark 3:22-26).

**Explaining the development.** Views include: (1) progressive revelation — the Old Testament gives glimpses, the New Testament fuller disclosure; (2) historical development under the pressure of suffering and exile, possibly influenced by Persian dualism (Zoroastrianism's evil spirit Angra Mainyu) — a once-popular theory now often treated cautiously; (3) both, in different proportions.

encounters.title: The accuser tests Job
encounters.summary: The satan questions whether Job's piety is disinterested. God permits the test but sets its limits.

encounters.title: The LORD rebukes the satan
encounters.summary: The accuser opposes Joshua the high priest; God rebukes him and clothes Joshua in clean garments — a picture of forgiveness overruling accusation.

encounters.title: Who incited David?
encounters.summary: Two accounts of David's census attribute the prompting to the LORD and to Satan, inviting reflection on God's sovereignty and evil agency.

encounters.title: The tempter in the wilderness
encounters.summary: Jesus resists the devil's three temptations by quoting Deuteronomy.

encounters.title: The accuser thrown down
encounters.summary: Revelation pictures the accuser cast out of heaven; Paul asks, 'Who shall bring any charge against God's elect?' because Christ intercedes.

archaeology.find: Dead Sea Scrolls: War Scroll and Rule of the Community
archaeology.summary: These texts describe Belial, the Angel of Darkness, leading the 'sons of darkness' against the 'sons of light', showing how Jewish ideas of a chief evil spirit had developed by the 1st century BC.

renamed.explanation: The definite article in Job and Zechariah shows a role, like 'the prosecutor'. By 1 Chr 21:1 and the New Testament, the word functions as a name.

laterFate: Christian theology developed detailed teaching about Satan's fall, power and defeat. Medieval art gave him horns and a tail borrowed partly from the Greek god Pan. Milton's *Paradise Lost* shaped much of the popular picture. Modern theologians differ over how literally to take Satan's personhood; most traditional churches affirm it.

name: Leviathan and Rahab
original: Hebrew liwyatan ('coiled one'); rahab ('raging, arrogant'); compare Ugaritic ltn (Lotan)
domains: forces opposed to God's ordered creation
symbol of hostile empires (Egypt as Rahab)
symbol: A many-headed sea serpent or dragon

cultCenter.name: No cult; Ugarit, where the Lotan texts were found

plain: Leviathan and Rahab are names for chaos monsters of the sea in Hebrew poetry. The Bible borrows imagery from older Canaanite myths, in which the storm god defeats a seven-headed sea serpent, and says that it is Israel's God who crushed the sea monster's heads. The images are used for creation, the Exodus, the defeat of hostile empires, and the final victory over evil.
myth: In the Ugaritic Baal Cycle (c. 1300 BC), Mot reminds Baal that he 'smote Lotan, the fleeing serpent, finished off the twisting serpent, the mighty one with seven heads'. The goddess Anat also boasts of defeating the sea god Yam and the dragon. In the Babylonian *Enuma Elish*, Marduk splits the sea monster Tiamat to make the world. Across the ancient Near East, the sea stood for chaos that a warrior god had to tame before order could exist.
biblicalRole:
**God the dragon-slayer.** 'You divided the sea by your strength; you broke the heads of the dragons in the waters. You crushed the heads of Leviathan' (Ps 74:13-14). 'Was it not you who cut Rahab in pieces, who pierced the dragon?' (Isa 51:9), immediately followed by the drying of the sea at the Exodus (Isa 51:10). By his power God 'stilled the sea' and 'by his understanding smote through Rahab' (Job 26:12-13; Ps 89:10).

**The end of chaos.** 'In that day the LORD with his sore and great and strong sword shall punish Leviathan the piercing (fleeing) serpent, Leviathan that crooked (twisting) serpent' (Isa 27:1) — almost word for word the Ugaritic description of Lotan, now projected into the future. Revelation pictures a great red dragon with seven heads (Rev 12:3) and a beast from the sea with seven heads (Rev 13:1), and the new creation has 'no more sea' (Rev 21:1).

**Tamed and playful.** Other passages reduce the monster: Leviathan is a creature God made to play in the sea (Ps 104:26), and God's speech in Job 41 describes Leviathan in awe-inspiring detail as a creature no human can tame, but God can (Job 41:1-34). Gen 1:21 says God *created* the great sea creatures (tanninim) — no battle needed.

**Rahab as Egypt.** Rahab becomes a nickname for Egypt: 'Rahab who sits still' (Isa 30:7), listed among nations that will know God (Ps 87:4). (This Rahab is unrelated to Rahab of Jericho, whose name is spelled differently in Hebrew.)

**How literal?** Some readers think the Bible affirms real primeval monsters; most scholars read these passages as poetic polemic: taking the imagery of Canaanite and Babylonian myth and declaring that Yahweh alone, not Baal or Marduk, rules the chaos. Some creationist writers identify Leviathan with a sea reptile or dinosaur; most interpreters, including many conservatives, see Job 41 as poetic, possibly drawing on the crocodile. Debated.

encounters.title: Crushing the heads of Leviathan
encounters.summary: A lament remembers God's ancient victory over the sea monsters as grounds for hope when the temple lies in ruins.

encounters.title: Leviathan punished in that day
encounters.summary: Isaiah uses language almost identical to the Ugaritic Lotan text to announce God's final defeat of evil.

encounters.title: Awake, arm of the LORD
encounters.summary: The defeat of Rahab is fused with the crossing of the Red Sea and the coming return from exile.

encounters.title: Can you draw out Leviathan with a hook?
encounters.summary: God humbles Job by describing a creature no human can master. In Psalm 104 the same creature is God's plaything.

encounters.title: Egypt called Rahab
encounters.summary: The chaos-monster name becomes a mocking title for Egypt: big and noisy, but useless as an ally.

encounters.title: The seven-headed dragon and no more sea
encounters.summary: Revelation brings the old chaos-dragon imagery to its climax and identifies the dragon with Satan.

archaeology.summary: The Ugaritic description of Lotan as the 'fleeing serpent', 'twisting serpent' with seven heads is so close to Isa 27:1 that scholars agree the prophet is using inherited imagery.

archaeology.find: Seven-headed dragon on an early Mesopotamian seal and shell plaque
archaeology.year: 1930s (Oriental Institute excavations in the Diyala region)
archaeology.summary: Third-millennium BC images show a god or hero fighting a seven-headed serpent, centuries before the Ugaritic and biblical texts.
Marduk's battle with Tiamat, the sea, is the Babylonian form of the chaos-battle motif.

renamed.explanation: The Ugaritic and Hebrew names come from the same root meaning 'coiled' or 'twisted'. The Hebrew form is not a hostile renaming but the same word in a different language.

laterFate: Jewish tradition imagined Leviathan served as food at the messianic banquet (for example in *2 Baruch* 29:4 and the Talmud). Thomas Hobbes used 'Leviathan' (1651) as the title of his book on the all-powerful state. In modern Hebrew, livyatan means 'whale'.
